listening.title: Fishing quotas and the tragedy of the commons
listening.titleVi: Hạn ngạch đánh bắt cá và bi kịch của tài sản chung
listening.context: An economics lecturer explains why open-access fishing leads to overfishing and how tradable quotas have been used to address it.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about fishing quotas. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today I want to look at a problem that economists call the tragedy of the commons, and at one of the most debated solutions to it in the world's fisheries: the use of quotas.

Let's begin with the basic problem. Fish in the open sea belong to nobody. Anyone with a boat and a net can go out and catch them, a situation economists call open access. That sounds fair, but it has a serious flaw.

Imagine you are the captain of a fishing boat. You know that the stocks are declining. If you decide to catch less in order to protect the fish, it makes no difference to the fish, because the other captains will simply catch whatever you leave behind. So, for each individual, the rational decision is to catch as much as possible before the competition does. When every captain thinks in this way, the fish disappear. This outcome is what we call the tragedy of the commons.

For a long time, governments responded with rules about equipment. They limited the size of nets, or the number of days that boats could go to sea. In practice, this rarely worked. Fishermen simply bought bigger engines and better sonar equipment, and caught the same amount of fish in fewer days.

From the nineteen seventies, some countries tried a different approach. Scientists estimate how much fish can be taken each year without damaging the breeding population, and the government then sets a total allowable catch, based on that advice. That total is divided into individual quotas, so that each boat has a legal right to land a certain weight of fish, and no more.

There was a second problem with equipment rules, and that was enforcement. Inspectors cannot be on every boat, and a captain who is already close to bankruptcy has a strong temptation to ignore the regulations. A system that depends on constant policing is expensive, and it is rarely popular with the fishing community.

Let me use a small northern country as an example, which I'll call Norvik. Norvik introduced individual quotas in the late nineteen eighties. People often assume that the quotas were sold from the very beginning, but that was not the case. At first, they were given free to boat owners, in proportion to their past catches. The captains who had caught the most fish received the largest quotas.

The crucial feature of the system was that quotas could be traded. An owner with a small quota who was struggling to make a profit could sell it to someone who could use it more productively. Over time, this meant that fishing became concentrated in the most efficient boats, which could catch the same amount of fish with less fuel and fewer crew.

Notice what this changes. Under open access, a captain has no reason to look after the fish, because anything he leaves will be taken by someone else. Under a quota system, the right to catch a share of the stock is something valuable that he owns, and its value depends on the stock staying healthy. In other words, the incentive points in a completely different direction.

However, quotas created a new difficulty. Each boat can land only a fixed weight of fish. So if a boat catches a small, low-value fish, that fish uses up quota that could have been used for a larger and more valuable one. The sensible commercial decision is to throw the small fish back into the sea, where they usually die. This practice is called discarding, and it is one of the most wasteful side effects of the whole system.

Enforcement did not disappear altogether, of course. Norvik placed independent observers on a sample of boats, and later installed cameras, to check that captains were reporting their catches honestly. These measures added to the cost, but the government considered that the cost was justified.

It is worth pausing here to ask why governments accepted this extra expense. The answer is that the alternative was far more costly. When a fishery collapses, thousands of jobs are lost in boatyards, processing plants and harbour towns, and it can take decades for the stock to return, if it returns at all. Prevention, in this case, is much cheaper than a cure.

So what were the results in Norvik? The most obvious change was the size of the fleet. At the start there were about eight hundred boats. Ten years later there were around five hundred. That was a dramatic fall, and it caused real hardship in some communities.

But for the fish, the news was good. Scientists had predicted that it would take at least twenty-five years for the cod to recover. In fact, within fifteen years, cod stocks in Norvik's waters had returned to a safe level, which was a pleasant surprise for everyone involved.

Interestingly, the change also altered how people behaved at sea. Under the old system, boats raced out of harbour at the start of the season and took as much as they could in a few frantic weeks. Fish arrived in the markets all at once, and prices collapsed. With quotas, captains could choose their moment, and the fish were landed over many months. As a result, consumers could buy fresh fish all year round, and the average price rose.

Not everyone is convinced, however, and critics make two main points. The first is social. Over time, the quotas ended up in the hands of a few large companies. Family-run boats that had sold their quota during a bad year often couldn't afford to buy it back, so coastal villages lost their traditional way of life, and the profits went to owners who lived far away.

In response, some governments now reserve a proportion of the total quota for small boats, and this share cannot be sold to the large operators. This gives the villages a degree of security, although it also reduces the efficiency gains that quotas are supposed to deliver.

The second criticism concerns fairness. If the government simply gives quotas away, it hands a very valuable asset to the existing owners for nothing. Many economists therefore argue that quotas should be sold at auction, so that the public receives a fair return for what is, after all, a public resource. Others reply that auctions would push small operators out even faster, so the debate is far from over.

Please also note that the figures I have quoted come from a simplified case, and real fisheries are usually messier. For next week, I'd like you to read the two articles on the course page, and think about which system you would choose if you were advising a government today.

listening.title: Reporting a home internet fault
listening.titleVi: Báo lỗi đường truyền internet gia đình
listening.context: A woman phones her internet provider to report a fault with her home broadband connection.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning her internet provider to report a fault. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, you're through to Brightline Broadband technical support. My name's Callum. How can I help you today?
Hello. I'm calling because my internet keeps cutting out, and I'm getting really fed up with it.
I'm sorry to hear that. Let's see what we can do. Could I take your name first, please?
Yes, it's Sandra Prescott. That's P, R, E, S, C, O, T, T.
Thank you, Ms Prescott. And could you confirm the address of the property for me?
It's forty-eight Linden Road. Linden is spelled L, I, N, D, E, N.
Got it. I can see your account on the screen now. Is the best number to reach you the mobile ending in four one three?
Yes, that's right. The full number is 07700 900 413.
Before we go on, can I ask whether I will be charged for this? A friend of mine had to pay when an engineer came to her house.

Not in your case. If the fault is on our network, the visit is free of charge. You would only pay if the problem turned out to be inside your home and caused by something you had installed yourself. We'll see on the day.
One more question. Will I lose my internet phone line while you are fixing this? My mother rings me every afternoon, and she gets worried if she cannot get through.

Your phone line runs on a different service, so it should keep working. If it does go quiet for a short time during the visit, the engineer will tell you beforehand, and it will come back as soon as he has finished.
That's a relief. Thank you.
Perfect. Now, tell me about the problem. Is the connection down all the time, or does it come and go?

It comes and goes, mostly. During the day it's fine, but it cuts out every evening, usually between seven and ten o'clock. That's exactly when I want to watch something or help my son with his homework.
That's very useful to know. When did it first start happening?
Let me think. It was last Wednesday, I'm sure, because I'd just come back from a work trip. So I suppose it's about four days now. No, wait, today is Monday, so that makes it five days.
Five days, thank you. Now, I'd like you to look at your router for me. It's the small white box that the internet cable plugs into. Can you see it?
Yes, it's right here on the shelf in the hall.
Are there any lights on the front? Normally there should be a steady green light.
There's a light on the front that's flashing orange. It was green when we first got it, so I suppose that isn't good.
No, orange suggests that the signal is unstable. It's not a problem with your equipment as such, so I think we need to send an engineer to check the line.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: How soon can someone come? I'm working from home on most days, so I can be here whenever you like.
Let me check the diary. I can offer you this Wednesday morning.
Oh, I'm afraid I can't do Wednesday. I have a dentist's appointment that I've already moved once. What about Thursday?
Thursday is fine. The engineers work in two-hour windows, so the visit will be on Thursday between eight and ten in the morning.
Eight o'clock is a bit early for us. Is there anything later?
Yes, there's another slot that morning, from ten until twelve.
Ten until twelve sounds better. Please book that one.
Done. So the engineer will arrive between ten and twelve on Thursday. Please make sure that somebody aged eighteen or over is at home.
That's no problem. Do I need to do anything beforehand?
Just keep the shelf in the hall clear so he can reach the router and the socket behind it. And if you could leave the router switched on, that would be a help.
Of course. And who will be coming? I'd like to tell my neighbour in case I'm out in the garden.
The engineer's name is Mr Brennan. That's B, R, E, N, N, A, N. He'll carry a photo identity card, so you can ask to see it.
Good. Is there anything I can quote if I need to ring back?
Yes. I'm giving your fault a reference number. It's T, S, and then the number nine, zero, four, one, seven.
Let me read that back. T S, nine zero four one seven. Perfect.
That's right. You'll also get a text message on your mobile with all of these details in a few minutes.

listening.title: A guided walk in a nature reserve
listening.titleVi: Hướng dẫn chuyến đi bộ trong khu bảo tồn thiên nhiên
listening.context: A ranger at Fernbrook Nature Reserve welcomes a walking group and explains the rules and the route.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a ranger giving a talk to a group of walkers at a nature reserve. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Fernbrook Nature Reserve. My name is Ruth, and I'll be your guide for this morning's walk.

Before we set off, let me tell you a little about the place. The reserve covers two hundred and ten hectares. When it was first proposed, the plan was for three hundred and forty, but the farmland at the northern end was never bought, so we ended up with a smaller site.
Even so, it is home to more than a thousand species of plants and animals, from tiny beetles to red deer.

Many visitors arrive at midday and wonder why they never see any deer. The truth is that the deer rest in the woods in the middle of the day. If you want to see them, the best time is early morning, just after sunrise, when they come out to graze at the edge of the meadow.
Dusk is also an interesting time, but that is when we see the bats, not the deer.
Now, a few rules. Dogs are welcome on the main paths, provided they are kept on a lead. Only the marsh area is completely closed to dogs, because it is so important for ground-nesting birds.

You may have noticed that the East Path is closed. A sign at the gate says that it is flooded. In fact, that sign is out of date. The water went down in the spring. The real reason is that a pair of nightjars is nesting beside the path, and we cannot risk disturbing them. We expect to reopen it in August.

Finally, a word about money. Parking is free, and so is entry, but we do rely on donations. The machine in the car park is out of order at the moment, so if you would like to give something, please use the box in the visitor centre. Every pound goes towards looking after the paths.

A few words about the weather and what to wear. The forecast is dry but cool, and the paths can be muddy in places, even after a week without rain, because the woodland holds the moisture. Sturdy shoes are strongly recommended, and I notice a couple of you are wearing trainers. You'll be fine, but you may get wet feet.
Please take all your litter home with you. We have no bins on the paths, because they attract foxes and crows, which in turn disturb the nesting birds. If you carry something in, please carry it out.

The reserve is run by a small team of five rangers and almost sixty volunteers. Many of our volunteers are retired teachers and engineers, and they do everything from counting butterflies to repairing fences. If you enjoy today, ask at the visitor centre about joining them. The only requirement is a free morning every fortnight and a willingness to get a little muddy.

The visitor centre also has a small shop and a café, which serves soup and home-made cakes. It opens at nine and closes at four thirty, so you will have time for a drink and a look round when we get back.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me explain the route. Please take the map from your pack. Our walk has five stops, which are marked on the map with numbers, and it takes about two and a half hours, at a gentle pace.

Our first stop is Mill Pond. As the name suggests, there was once a flour mill beside the pond. The building has long gone, but you can still see the old stone foundations and part of the wheel pit. There are picnic tables here as well, but we will be using those for our lunch break at the end, not now.

From there we follow the stream to the second stop, Willow Bridge. This is one of the quietest spots in the reserve. If we stand still and say nothing for a few minutes, we have a good chance of seeing an otter. They have been fishing here regularly since last winter.
You might have read in our leaflet that dragonflies are common in the reserve. They are, but only around the marsh, which we will not be visiting today, so please don't be disappointed.

The third stop is Heron Hide. It is a wooden shelter overlooking the lake, and it is a lovely place to sit and watch the water birds. But what many people miss is the meadow right in front of it. In June, wild orchids come into flower there, and several of them are quite rare. Please stay on the boardwalk so that we don't trample them.

After a short climb, we reach the fourth stop, Quarry Ledge. This is a disused quarry, and it gives us a rare chance to see the layers of rock that make up the valley. There is an information board here that explains how the rocks were formed, and I think you'll find it fascinating.

And our last stop is Beacon Hill, the highest point in the reserve. On a clear day like today, you can see right across the estuary to the sea. It is the favourite spot of our photographers, so have your cameras ready.

One more thing about the final stretch. The path down from the hill is steep and rocky for the first two hundred metres, so please take your time. If anyone feels tired at any point, tell me, and we can slow down or take a shorter way back along the road. There is no rush, and nobody will be left behind.
I will carry a first-aid kit and a radio, and my mobile phone has a good signal on the hill, but not in the valley, so please do not wander off on your own.
From the top, it is an easy walk down to the picnic tables at the pond, where we will finish with a hot drink.
Does anyone have any questions before we start? No? In that case, please follow me.

listening.title: Planning a geology field trip
listening.titleVi: Lên kế hoạch chuyến thực địa địa chất
listening.context: Two geology students and their tutor discuss the arrangements for a two-day field trip.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two geology students, Jake and Marcus, talking to their tutor, Dr Hall, about a field trip. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, you've sent me your outline for the field trip. Jake, I see you've suggested Cliffmoor as the location.
Yes. It's only forty minutes from campus, so we'd save a lot of travelling time, and the cliffs there are easy to reach.
But when we looked at it more carefully, we realised that Tarn Valley is a better choice for our project.
Why is that, Marcus?

Well, at Cliffmoor you only see one kind of rock. At Tarn Valley you can see sedimentary, igneous and metamorphic rocks all within a couple of kilometres. That's exactly what we need for comparing how they formed.
I agree. Tarn Valley it is, even though it's a longer journey. Now, how are you planning to get there? I see you wrote down the train.
That was our first idea. But the nearest station is eight kilometres from the first site, and we'd be carrying heavy sample bags and equipment.
So you've changed your minds?
Yes. The department has a minibus that we can borrow for the weekend. It's much more practical, and the cost is only the petrol.
Good. I'll make sure the booking is confirmed. What about accommodation? I remember you were thinking about a campsite.
We were, because it's cheap. But the forecast is for heavy rain and cold nights, so camping is out of the question.
There's a youth hostel in the village. It's a bit more expensive, but it has a drying room for wet clothes and boots, which is a big advantage.
That sounds wise. A bed-and-breakfast would be too costly for the whole group.
How many people will be coming in total? Last year the second-year group was too large for the minibus, and I don't want a repeat of that.
There are eleven of us, plus you. The minibus takes fourteen, so we have enough space, although the bags will be a bit of a squeeze.
We could put the bags in the boot and the sample boxes under the seats. It worked well on the day trip to the coast last term.
As long as the aisle stays clear. I'm quite strict about that. Another point is food. Will you be cooking at the hostel?
The hostel has a kitchen, so we thought we'd all share the cooking and split the cost. It's a lot cheaper than eating out every evening.
Good plan. Please check whether anyone has special dietary needs, so that nobody is left out.
Is there anything we need to do before the trip is approved, Dr Hall?

Yes. It's the most important thing, actually. The university will not approve any field trip until you have submitted a risk assessment. Insurance is arranged by the department, and I'll deal with the minibus, so you just need to concentrate on the form. I need it by the end of next week.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, equipment. Some students forget the basics. Are you taking hammers to collect samples?
I'd planned to, yes.
I'm afraid that's not allowed in Tarn Valley. Part of it is a protected site, so you may only collect loose rocks from the stream bed. Hammers must stay at home.
OK. What about hard hats? We'll be near the quarry face.
The department will provide those, so there's no need to bring your own. What you do need is a hand lens for looking at mineral grains closely. You'd be surprised how many people forget them.
I've got one. And a waterproof notebook is a good idea, I suppose, in case the rain gets heavy?
Definitely. Ordinary paper will be useless if it gets wet. A camera is useful, but your phone will be fine, so you don't need to buy one.
Dr Hall, what should we write up when we get back? Is it a full report or a shorter field notebook?

Both, in a way. Your field notebooks are assessed first, and they count for forty per cent of the module. I will look at them for neatness and accuracy, not just for good handwriting. Then there is a group report, which should be around three thousand words.
That's quite a lot of work for one weekend. Can we start the report during the trip?

I would encourage you to, at least a rough outline each evening at the hostel, while everything is still fresh in your memory. Students who wait until they are back on campus often forget the small details, and those details are exactly what earn the higher marks.
We'll do that. We might also take turns, so that one person writes up each day's results.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Finally, let's look at the timetable for the two days. Marcus, what have you put for the first morning?
We'll arrive at about ten, so on Saturday morning we'll start by measuring the rock layers in the quarry. We can record the thickness of each layer and its angle.
Good. And in the afternoon?

I wanted to sketch the cliff section, but Marcus pointed out that the forecast is best on Saturday, and a sketch can be done in any weather. So in the afternoon we'll collect samples from the stream bed instead, while it is dry.
That makes sense. The forecast is better on Saturday. What about Sunday?
On Sunday morning, we'll walk to the fault line and map it, using our compasses. We should be able to see where the rocks on each side have moved.
Excellent. And Sunday afternoon?
We'd originally thought of photographing fossils in the limestone, but there may be too little time. Instead we plan to sketch the cliff section, since that can be done even if it rains.
What happens if the weather turns out worse than the forecast? We can't map a fault line in a thunderstorm.

Safety comes first. If there is lightning, or the stream rises, we stop and go back to the minibus. We would then swap the outdoor tasks for some laboratory work on the samples you have already collected. So you should pack plenty of sample bags and labels on the first day.
That's reassuring. I'd hate to waste the whole trip.
Fine. Then we need to be on the road by four o'clock to get back before dark. Send me the final timetable by Friday.

listening.title: How octopuses learn
listening.titleVi: Khả năng học tập của bạch tuộc
listening.context: A lecturer in animal behaviour explains what scientists have discovered about learning and intelligence in octopuses.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about how octopuses learn. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. In today's lecture I'd like to talk about an animal that has surprised biologists for decades: the octopus. Most of us think of intelligence as something that belongs to mammals and birds, and yet this soft-bodied creature, related to snails and clams, can solve problems in ways that seem almost human.

Let me begin with the brain. An octopus has roughly five hundred million neurons, which is similar to a dog and far more than any other invertebrate. What is unusual is where those cells are found. Only about a third are in the central brain. Around two thirds are in the arms.

This means that each arm can, to some extent, make its own decisions. If an arm is touching something, it can taste it, decide whether it is food, and pass it towards the mouth without waiting for instructions from the brain. Some researchers describe an octopus as having nine brains, although that is a slight exaggeration.

Now, you might expect an animal this clever to live a long time. In fact, most octopuses live for only about two years, and some species less than that. This has a remarkable consequence. Most clever animals, such as chimpanzees or crows, learn a lot from their parents. Baby octopuses never do. The mother lays her eggs, guards them for months without eating, and dies soon after they hatch. So the young have to learn everything alone.

How do we know what they can learn? In laboratories, researchers have given octopuses a series of tasks. One of the best known involves a jar with a screw-top lid. A crab is placed inside, in full view. At first the octopus simply grabs at the glass. After a few attempts, it works out that the lid turns, and within a few days it can open the jar in a minute or two. It then remembers how to do it, even weeks later.

Researchers have also trained octopuses to tell shapes apart. They are rewarded with food when they choose, say, a circle, and given a mild disturbance when they choose a square. Soon they reliably pick the circle. This type of learning is called association, and it is common in many animals.

Another example concerns escape. Keepers in aquariums tell many stories of octopuses that vanish from their tanks at night. An octopus has no bones, so it can squeeze through any gap that is larger than its beak, which is the only hard part of its body. Some have been found in neighbouring tanks, having helped themselves to the fish there, and then returned home before the staff arrived in the morning.

This ability to solve problems is helped by its sense of touch. The suckers on each arm contain thousands of receptors that are sensitive to taste and texture. So when an octopus explores a crevice, it is not only feeling the shape of the space, but also working out what is inside it. Vision matters too, and octopuses have excellent eyes, although, oddly enough, they cannot see colour. How they manage such convincing camouflage remains a puzzle.

What is more unusual is that individual octopuses behave differently from each other, even when they are the same species and live in identical tanks. Some are bold and come straight out to investigate a new object. Others hide for hours. Keepers have noticed that these differences are stable over time, which suggests that each animal has something like a personality.

Now let's turn to tool use, which is generally seen as a sign of high intelligence. In the wild, a species called the veined octopus has been filmed collecting halves of discarded coconut shells from the sea floor. It carries them across open ground, often walking awkwardly on the tips of its arms, and when danger threatens, it assembles the two halves around its body like a shelter. The octopus gains nothing at the time it picks up the shells. The benefit comes later, which means it must be planning ahead.

Another surprising behaviour is play. In one well-known case, captive octopuses were given an empty plastic bottle. Some of them squirted jets of water at it, so that it floated to the far side of the tank and then drifted back, and they repeated this again and again. There was no food and no obvious reward. Many scientists believe that this was simply for fun, a behaviour that is rare outside birds and mammals.

Let me say a little more about memory, because it is so important to everything I have described. Octopuses seem to have two systems. A short-term system lets them remember what happened a few minutes ago, such as which crab they have just tried. A longer-term system, which depends on a specific region of the brain called the vertical lobe, holds the lessons learned over weeks. When researchers damaged this region in experimental animals, the octopuses could still move and hunt, but they could no longer keep their new knowledge.

There is also evidence that octopuses may learn by watching. In a classic experiment, one group of octopuses saw a neighbour choose a particular coloured ball for a reward, and when they were given the same choice, they preferred the same colour. Not every researcher accepts this result, and the experiment has been difficult to repeat, so we should treat it with caution.

What are the main difficulties in studying octopus learning? The first is that they are rather hard to motivate. An octopus that finds a task dull simply stops taking part. A rat will keep pressing a lever for hours, but an octopus quickly becomes bored, so researchers must keep inventing new puzzles. A second problem is that individual differences are so large that results from one animal may tell us little about another.

There is a third problem, which is that we simply do not know how to compare an octopus with a mammal. Their last common ancestor lived more than five hundred million years ago, and was probably a simple worm-like animal. So octopus intelligence evolved completely separately from ours. Some scientists call it the closest thing we have to meeting an intelligent alien, and I think that description is not far wrong.

This makes the questions we ask extremely important. If we test an octopus using human ideas about what is clever, we may miss abilities that are impressive but quite different from our own. Good research starts by observing what the animal does naturally, and only then designs the experiment.

Finally, there is an ethical dimension. Because the evidence suggests that these animals can feel pain and have experiences, a number of countries now include octopuses in the legislation that protects animals used in research. Scientists must show that their experiments are necessary, and that the animals suffer as little as possible.
Next week we'll compare the octopus with its relatives, the squid and the cuttlefish, and ask whether intelligence has evolved more than once in the animal kingdom.

listening.title: Joining a language exchange club
listening.titleVi: Gia nhập câu lạc bộ trao đổi ngôn ngữ
listening.context: A woman phones a language exchange club to join a weekly conversation group.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a language exchange club to join a conversation group. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, Tandem Table Language Exchange, Joel speaking.
Oh, hello. I found your leaflet in the library, and I'd like to join one of your conversation groups. Is that possible?
Of course. We have a few hundred members now, and the club has been running for about eight years. Most people hear about us from a friend, so it's nice that the leaflet is working too.
I picked it up when I was returning some books. It looked friendlier than the formal language courses I've tried before.
Of course. New members are always welcome. I'll just open the registration form. Can I take your name first?
Yes, it's Marta Lindqvist.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Sure. It's L, I, N, D, Q, V, I, S, T. It's Swedish, and everyone gets it wrong.
Got it. And a mobile number, please?
It's oh double seven double oh, nine one four, three five eight.
Let me check that. Oh double seven double oh, nine one four, three five six?
No, three five eight.
Three five eight. Thank you. Now, which language would you like to practise?
Well, I studied French at school, but I haven't used it for years. What I really want is Italian, because I'm moving to Turin next spring for work.
Lovely. We have lots of Italian speakers, so you shouldn't have any trouble finding a partner. And how would you describe your level?
Um, upper-intermediate? Actually, no. I'd better be honest. After a year of evening classes, I'd call myself intermediate. I can read quite well, but I freeze when people speak quickly.
That's very common, and it's exactly what the group is for.
I'm a bit nervous, to be honest. I worry that I'll make mistakes and the other person will be bored.

Nobody minds mistakes here. Everybody is learning something, so you'll find people are very patient. Our rule is that you correct a partner only if they ask you to. Now, we meet on Wednesday and Thursday evenings. Which would suit you?
Wednesday would be better, if there's room.
I'm afraid the Wednesday group is full at the moment. There's a waiting list. The Thursday group has plenty of space, though.
Thursday is fine, then. I can rearrange my class.
Great. Now, the joining fee is twenty pounds, but for students it's only fifteen. Are you a student at all?
I'm doing a part-time master's degree, so yes, I am.
Then it's fifteen pounds. You can pay on your first night. Just bring your student card.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Where does the Thursday group meet? Is it at the library?
We used to meet in the library, but it got too noisy for the other readers. Now it's at the Juniper Café, in the upstairs room. It's quite near the station.
The Juniper Café. I know it. What time do I need to arrive?

The doors open at seven, so people can order drinks and say hello, but the conversation starts at half past seven. Please try not to be late, because we begin with a short game to get everyone talking.
How long does the evening last?

About an hour and a half in total. We work in pairs, and you speak for twenty minutes in one language, then switch and spend twenty minutes in the other. After that, everyone mixes with different partners.
That sounds very well organised.

There are usually around twenty members, from all sorts of backgrounds. We have nurses, engineers, a couple of retired teachers and quite a few students, and the conversation topics are always chosen by the pairs themselves.
And if I can't come one week, do I have to tell you in advance?
A short message is helpful, but you don't have to give a reason. Just send a text to the club number, so that we can match your partner with somebody else.
Is there anything I should prepare in advance? Perhaps a few topics, so that I don't go silent in front of my partner?

It's a nice idea, but don't worry too much. Some people bring a photograph or a newspaper article to start the conversation. Others simply talk about their week. Either way, you'll be fine once you've begun.
I'll bring a photograph of Turin, then. At least I'll have something to ask about.
One more thing. When you join, you'll get a membership card, and that gets you a free coffee on your first night.
Oh, that's kind. Thank you very much, Joel. I'll see you on Thursday.
Looking forward to it, Marta. Goodbye.

listening.title: Open day at a community garden
listening.titleVi: Buổi giới thiệu ngày hội mở cửa vườn cộng đồng
listening.context: The coordinator of a community garden briefs volunteers before the garden’s annual open day.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the coordinator of a community garden talking to volunteers about its open day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Hello, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Ruth, the coordinator here at Larkfield Community Garden, and I'm very grateful that so many of you have offered to help with Saturday's open day.
I know some of you have been volunteering for years, while others have only just joined, so I'll try to make sure that everybody leaves this meeting knowing exactly what to expect.

For those of you who are new, let me say a little about how the garden began. Ten years ago, this whole area was a disused bowling green. The council was about to sell it for building land, but a group of neighbours persuaded them to lease it to us instead.

Over the years we've added a lot. The greenhouse, for example, is our proudest achievement. Most of the money for it was raised at our annual plant sale. The council grant that we received last year only paid for the new fencing.
We now have sixty plots, and members rent a plot for one year at a time. There's a long waiting list, so if you hear someone say they're hoping to get one, please don't promise them anything.

Our gardeners come from every part of the neighbourhood. We have a retired bus driver who grows the biggest pumpkins I've ever seen, a family who share one plot between three generations, and a group of students who experiment with vegetables from all over the world. That mixture is what makes the garden special, and I'd like visitors on Saturday to feel it.

Now, Saturday. We're expecting around five hundred visitors, which is far more than we've ever had. The biggest problem will be parking. Elm Road is very narrow and the residents have already complained, so we're asking everyone to park at the primary school, which has kindly opened its playground for the day. It's only a five-minute walk.

Some people have suggested a shuttle bus, but it would cost too much and we'd need a driver, so we've decided against it. We're encouraging people to cycle if they can, and there'll be bike racks by the entrance.

Please be polite to anyone who asks you about the traffic. Our neighbours have been very patient with us over the years, and we'd like to keep it that way. If a resident does complain, don't argue. Just take their name, and I'll call them on Monday.

As for you, the volunteers, I'd like you all here by nine. No, sorry, I need to correct that. Half past eight, because the stalls take longer to set up than you'd think. There'll be tea and toast for everyone. You'll each be given a green apron so visitors can easily recognise you.

During the day, you'll work in shifts of about two hours, so that nobody gets tired. If you need a break, there are chairs by the shed, and a first-aid kit is kept in the hall. Please remember to drink plenty of water, even if it rains.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me explain where everything will be. Have a look at the plan of the garden on your sheet. As visitors come in through the main gate, they'll find the registration table straight away, where we hand out leaflets. That's the only thing near the entrance, so we want the crowd to move on quickly.

The seed swap will be under the apple trees. People bring packets of seeds from their own gardens and swap them. It's the most popular activity every year, so I've given it the biggest space, with plenty of shade.
The bee demonstration will take place behind the shed. Our beekeeper, Anil, will open a hive, and for safety visitors must stay behind a rope, so we need a quiet area away from the paths.
Next, the compost workshop. You might think compost isn't very exciting, but it always attracts a crowd. It'll be beside the greenhouse, because the heaps are right there.

The workshop is led by Mehmet, who has looked after our compost for six years. He promises to explain it without any difficult scientific words, and he usually gives away a small bag of the finished product to anyone who asks a good question.
The pond is a lovely spot, and people will want to look at it, but please don't put any stalls there. Frogs and small children don't mix well with crowds.
The children's den-building will be by the herb spiral. We've collected lots of branches and old sheets. It's near enough for parents to see, but away from the busy paths.
And finally, refreshments. We'll serve soup, cakes and hot drinks in the community hall, because the forecast says it might rain, and we'd like people to have somewhere dry to sit.
Everything on the menu is made from ingredients grown in the garden or donated by local shops, and the cakes are baked by our members. All the money raised goes into next year's seeds and tools.

One last thing. Please take photographs on the day, and send your favourites to the garden's email address afterwards. We use them for our newsletter, and they help us to persuade people to support us next year.

Visitors will also be able to buy plants from the stall at the gate, and every pot has a label explaining how to look after it. If anyone asks you for advice, don't be shy. Tell them what you know, and if you aren't sure, ask one of the experienced gardeners.
Right. If there are no questions, let's go and put up the signs.

listening.title: Planning a film studies presentation
listening.titleVi: Lên kế hoạch bài thuyết trình nhóm môn phim học
listening.context: Two film studies students discuss a group presentation about a silent film with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two film studies students, Nadia and Callum, talking to their tutor, Dr Fenwick, about a group presentation. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Come in, both of you. So, you wanted to talk about your presentation on The Lantern Keeper. Remind me why you chose that film.
Mainly because it was made in nineteen twenty-six, just before sound arrived, so we thought we could look at how filmmakers used live music to shape the audience's feelings.
We did consider a later film, but the sources were mostly about directing and acting. Almost nothing on the music, which is what interests us.
Good. Original angle. And it has a strong story too, hasn't it? A lighthouse keeper trying to save a stranded ship.
Yes, there's plenty of tension, and the music has to follow every change of mood. But the story hasn't been the problem.
So what has been the main difficulty so far?
Finding out what music was actually played. The original scores for most cinemas were lost, and the surviving copy of the film has a modern soundtrack added to it.
That is a problem for any researcher. How are you handling it?
Well, we found a few old cinema programmes in the university archive. They list the pieces the orchestra played. It's not complete, but it's something.
Make sure you say clearly in the presentation which parts are evidence and which are your own interpretation. Examiners notice when students blur that line.
We'll put the programmes on one slide, so everybody can see exactly where our information comes from.
Excellent. And I assume you've both been worrying about the time limit?
Yes, it's only twenty minutes. At first I was afraid the clips would take up most of it, but Nadia worked out that we only need three short ones.
I timed them yesterday. Each one lasts about a minute, so there's still plenty of space for our own analysis, and we'll have a little time left for the question session.
Sensible. How will you divide the talk between you?
We thought of splitting it by time period, but it was a bit artificial. So we'll each take a theme instead, and then link them together at the end.

I think a theme-based structure suits your topic much better, as long as the links are smooth. A presentation sounds better when it feels like one argument and not two separate talks. Practise the handover at least twice before the day.
We're going to rehearse in the seminar room on Friday, so that we can check the sound system as well.
We've also asked two friends from the course to sit at the back and tell us if they can't hear us. It's easy to forget how quiet you sound in a big room.
Very wise. Many students speak far too quickly when they're nervous, so ask your friends to hold up a card if you do.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, on the sound itself, you can't cover everything in twenty minutes. Which aspects are you going to concentrate on?
I wanted to include silence, because there are some moments when the orchestra stopped altogether, and it's incredibly powerful.
It is certainly dramatic. But think carefully about the evidence you can really show to an audience before you decide.
That's interesting, but I think we've only found evidence for it in one scene, so we'd be speculating. What we have good evidence for is the music that signals which characters are good or bad.
True. And the other one has to be the way the music speeds up during the chase scenes. We can match that to the cinema programmes.
I agree. The speed of the music in chases is well documented. And what about sound effects? Cinemas often had people making them behind the screen.
We'd love to, but it would take too long to explain properly. Maybe we'll mention it in the question session.
Fair enough. Remember that the questions will be your chance to show how much you know, so keep a few interesting facts in reserve. Examiners always ask about the things you didn't have time to say.
We've actually prepared a short list of those, including the way the cinema owners hired the musicians.
And I'd like to bring a short recording of a modern orchestra playing one of the pieces, so the audience can hear the difference between fast and slow versions.
That's a lovely idea. Just check the copyright first. The library can help you with that.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Let me give you some feedback on your outline. Starting with the introduction. You've written a full page about the history of cinema in the twenties.
Yes. We thought the audience would need the background.

I understand why, but your classmates have all studied this period for a term already, and they will quickly lose interest. They already know it. Cut it down to a couple of sentences and spend the time on your argument.
OK. What about the clip analysis? We're planning to show each clip twice, once with sound and once without.
I like that very much. It makes the effect of the music obvious. Keep it just as it is.
And the section on audiences? We've included some quotations from newspaper reviews.
Hmm. Reviews are useful, but they're mostly from London. You need at least one from a small town, because the experience there would have been quite different.
That's a good point. And finally, the conclusion. We've said that music was more important than the pictures.
That's too strong a claim for a presentation of this size. Say it was one of the most important elements, and then you can defend it.
We hadn't thought of that. I suppose we've only been looking at the places where the evidence is easy to find.
Exactly, so be open about it. It's perfectly acceptable to say what you couldn't find out.
Thanks, Dr Fenwick. That gives us a lot to work on before the presentation.
Send me the revised outline by Thursday, and I'll reply as soon as I can. Good luck to you both.
Should we send the clips as well, or just the written outline?
Just the outline for now. I'll look at the clips when you rehearse, because I'll be in the seminar room on Friday anyway.
Then we'll see you there. Thank you again.

listening.title: Turning seawater into drinking water
listening.titleVi: Khử mặn nước biển để lấy nước uống
listening.context: A lecturer in environmental engineering explains how desalination works and what problems it causes.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about turning seawater into drinking water. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning, everyone. Today's topic is desalination, which simply means removing salt from seawater to make it fit to drink. As more of the world's cities face water shortages, it's becoming an increasingly important technology.

I'll divide the lecture into three parts. First the basic methods, then the environmental problems, and finally some developments that may change the industry in the coming years. Please save your questions until the end.

Let me begin with some basic chemistry. Seawater contains roughly thirty-five grams of salt in every litre. You couldn't drink it, because your kidneys would need more water to get rid of the salt than the seawater supplies.

The oldest method is distillation. You heat the seawater until it turns into steam, leaving the salt behind, and then you cool the steam so that it becomes fresh water again. Sailors were doing this on ships long before anyone built a large plant.

Even today, distillation is common in regions where fuel is cheap, particularly in countries with large reserves of oil and gas. In those places the extra energy is not seen as a problem, which is why some of the biggest distillation plants in the world are found there.

There is also a hybrid design, in which a plant produces electricity and fresh water together. The waste heat from the power station is used to evaporate the seawater, so very little energy is wasted. It works well, but it requires the two facilities to be built side by side, which is not always possible.

The trouble with distillation is that heating huge amounts of water uses an enormous amount of fuel. So over the last few decades, most new plants have switched to a different approach called reverse osmosis.

Here is how it works. Seawater is pushed at very high pressure against a thin membrane. The membrane has holes so tiny that water molecules can squeeze through, but salt cannot. The pressure needed is about fifty times normal atmospheric pressure. Sorry, I should say closer to sixty times, as the exact figure depends on how salty the water is.
Making that pressure takes a great deal of power. In a modern plant, the main running cost is energy, not labour and not the membranes themselves, which people often assume.

Engineers have improved efficiency a lot. Many plants now recover energy from the high-pressure brine that leaves the membranes and use it to help push in the next batch of seawater. A few decades ago, reverse osmosis needed more than three times as much electricity per litre as it does today.

The membranes do need regular cleaning, though, because tiny algae and minerals build up on the surface. Operators usually replace them every few years, which is a significant expense, but a smaller one than the electricity bill.
Now, desalination isn't a perfect solution, and there are three main environmental concerns. I'll deal with them one at a time.

The first is the leftover salty water, known as brine. For every litre of fresh water produced, roughly the same amount of brine is created, and it's about twice as salty as the sea. If you simply pour it back into the sea, it sinks to the bottom and can harm life on the seabed.

Engineers have found a way to reduce the damage. Instead of one big outlet, they use a long pipe with many small nozzles. The brine is sprayed out in all directions, so it mixes with the sea much faster.

Some plants go further and choose the site of the outlet carefully, putting it where strong currents will carry the brine away. Monitoring is also important. Operators measure the saltiness of the water around the outlet every day, and they adjust the flow if it starts to rise.

One interesting idea is to treat the brine as a resource rather than a waste product. It contains salt, magnesium and other minerals, and a few companies are already extracting some of them for sale. So far the quantities are small, but if the process becomes cheaper, it could help to pay for the plant.

The second concern is at the other end of the plant, where seawater is drawn in. The strong current can pull in small fish, eggs and tiny creatures, and kill them. To prevent this, plants now fit fine screens over the intake pipes, and they slow the water down so that most animals can swim away.

The third problem is greenhouse gases. If a plant is powered by coal or gas, then making a glass of water produces carbon dioxide. A growing number of plants avoid this by using solar energy, especially in sunny regions where the need for water is greatest.

This matters because desalinated water is already more expensive than water from rivers or underground sources. If energy prices rise, or if governments tax carbon, the gap would widen, so cleaner power is also an economic question and not just an environmental one.

Some countries have been more successful than others in making these choices. Where governments plan the supply of water and energy together, the results tend to be much better than where each is handled by a different department with different goals.

So what does the future hold? Much of the current research aims to make reverse osmosis cheaper by improving the membrane. The most exciting candidate is a membrane made from graphene, a material only one atom thick. In theory, water could pass through it with much less pressure, which would save a great deal of energy.

Another trend is towards small plants. Large plants are expensive to build and need long pipelines, so they suit big coastal cities. But smaller, solar-powered units are now being tested on remote islands, where bringing in water by ship is extremely costly.

These small units are usually built inside shipping containers, so they can be transported by lorry or boat and installed within a few days. If the trials succeed, a village could have its own supply without waiting years for a large public project.

Critics point out that cheap water might encourage waste. If a city believes the sea is an unlimited source, it may stop repairing leaking pipes or encouraging people to save water. Most experts therefore recommend that desalination should always go together with efforts to reduce demand.

To sum up, desalination can provide a reliable supply of water that doesn't depend on rainfall, but only if we deal with the energy it uses and the damage it does to the sea. In next week's lecture, we'll look at the alternative of recycling wastewater.

Before you leave, I'd like you to think about one question for the seminar. If desalination becomes cheap and clean, should cities near the coast still be asked to limit their water use? There are good arguments on both sides, and I'd like to hear them.

listening.title: Registering for temporary work
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký làm việc tạm thời qua công ty môi giới việc làm
listening.context: A man phones an employment agency to register for temporary warehouse work.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning an employment agency to register for temporary work. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, Brightway Staffing, Sandra speaking. How can I help you?
Morning. I'm looking for temporary work, and a friend told me I can register with you over the phone before I come in.
That's right, and it saves a lot of time on the day. I'll fill in your registration form while we talk. Could I take your full name, please?
It's Daniel Aldridge.
Is that Aldridge with an E on the end?
Yes, it is. A, L, D, R, I, D, G, E.
Thank you. And your address, Daniel?
Fourteen Camden Row, Norwich.
And the postcode?
N, R, four, seven, Q, T.
Lovely, I've got that. And may I ask how you heard about us?

My neighbour Karen registered with you last year, and she said you were always quick to find her work. She did a few weeks at a garden centre, and then a longer job at a food factory, and she was very happy with both.

That's nice to hear. Most of our new people come to us that way, through friends and family. Now, what kind of work are you looking for? We have vacancies in offices, in shops and in warehouses at the moment.
Well, my last job was in an office, doing data entry, so I was thinking of looking for something similar.
We do have several of those on our books this week, mostly in the city centre.
Actually, now that I think about it, I spent nine months sitting at a desk and I'd really like a change. I'd prefer something more active. Do you have anything in warehouses?
Plenty. Warehouse it is, then. And when would you be able to start?
My current contract finishes on the first of June, so I could start on the second.
OK, the second of June.
Oh, hang on. I've just remembered I'm going to my sister's wedding that weekend, so the third would be better.
No problem. Then the third of June it is. Do you hold any certificates that might help us place you?
Yes. I've got a forklift licence, which I got two years ago. I also did a first aid course, but that certificate has run out.

The forklift licence is very useful. Warehouses always want people who can drive one. Now, what about shifts? Warehouse work is usually early mornings, afternoons or nights, and nights pay a bit more.
I know nights pay more, but I have a young daughter, so mornings suit me best. I'm happy to start at six.
Early mornings, then. I'll note that down.
Is it far to travel? I don't own a car at the moment, so I'll be relying on buses.

Most of our warehouse clients are on the same industrial estate on the edge of the city, and there is a bus route that runs from the centre. Many of our people share lifts too, and we can put you in touch with others who live nearby once you start.
That would be really useful. Thank you.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Can you tell me what sort of pay to expect?
For general warehouse assistants, the rate is eleven pounds fifty an hour. Forklift drivers can earn up to thirteen pounds, but you would have to pass a short practical check first.
I see. So I'd start on the assistant rate. And is the pay weekly or monthly?
Temporary staff are paid weekly, every Friday, straight into your bank account. It's only permanent staff who are paid monthly, so don't be confused if your friends tell you something different.
That's helpful, thanks. What happens next? Do I have to come in?
Yes, we'd like to see you for a short interview on Thursday afternoon. We have to check your right to work in this country, so please bring proof of identity.
Is my driving licence enough? I don't have it with me all the time, but I could bring it.
Not on its own, I'm afraid. Bring your passport, because we have to take a copy of it for our records.
Fine, I'll bring that. Is there anything I need to buy before I start work?
The warehouse will give you a hi-vis jacket and a hard hat, but you need to buy your own safety boots. They must have steel toecaps.
OK, I'll get a pair this week. Thank you very much for your help, Sandra.

One last thing. Once you start, you will fill in an online timesheet each week, and I'll send you the link by email this afternoon. If the timesheet is late, the payment can be delayed, so please do it promptly.
Understood. I'll look out for the email.
You're welcome, Daniel. We'll look forward to seeing you on Thursday.

listening.title: A new community bus service
listening.titleVi: Tuyến xe buýt cộng đồng mới của thung lũng
listening.context: A local radio presenter reports on a new community bus route that starts next week.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter talking about a new community bus service. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Welcome back to Valley Voices. Now, a story that many of you have been waiting for. From next Monday, the villages around Harlow Green will finally have a community bus of their own. It's called Route Seven C, and I've been finding out how it will work.

Some background first. Six years ago the commercial bus company withdrew its service to the villages, saying there weren't enough passengers. Since then, anyone without a car has had to rely on lifts from neighbours or an expensive taxi to reach the town centre.
The new service is run by a charity, the Valley Link Trust, and not by the council. The council did promise some money in the spring, but it withdrew the offer when its own budget was cut.

So where does the money come from? By far the largest share comes from a grant from the regional transport fund. The rest comes from passenger fares and from donations by local businesses, but those are much smaller amounts.

Now, how often will the bus run? On weekdays, there will be a bus every thirty minutes, with the first one leaving Harlow Green at a quarter to seven in the morning. The trust had hoped to run one every twenty minutes, but that would have needed a third vehicle, and they simply can't afford it yet.
On Saturdays the service runs every hour, and I'm sorry to say that there will be no Sunday service for the time being. The trust will review that after six months.

What about fares? A single adult ticket costs one pound eighty, and a day ticket is four pounds. Pensioners pay half price. Children under five travel free, so families with very small children will save a good deal of money.

I know some listeners have asked about people with disabilities. At the moment there is no special reduction for passengers with a disability card, but the trust says it is looking at the question and will announce a decision in the new year.

Let's talk about the buses themselves. Originally the trust planned to buy two second-hand diesel buses, but in the end it chose two new minibuses, and both of them are fully electric. Each carries sixteen passengers and one wheelchair.
The vehicles will be charged overnight at a depot behind the old dairy, and the charging point there has been paid for by the supermarket on Church Road.

Finally, the trust needs help. It already has twelve trained volunteer drivers, so it does not need any more of those. What it is really short of is people to answer the booking phone line. Anyone who wants a wheelchair space or who needs to be collected from a house away from the route must book ahead, and someone has to take those calls between eight and five.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: So where exactly will the bus go? Let me take you along the route in order, and you can follow the map on the trust's leaflet.

The first stop is on Harlow Green itself, beside the farmers' market. The market takes place every Saturday morning, so the Saturday bus should be a popular way to go shopping for fresh vegetables and local cheese.

The bus then travels down Millbank Road, where the second stop is right outside the medical centre. This will be the most important stop for many older residents, who until now have had real difficulty getting to appointments.

The third stop is on Orchard Lane, next to the care home. The trust expects that visitors will be regular users, and the care home has agreed to let passengers wait in its entrance hall when the weather is bad.

After that, the bus turns on to the main road and stops at Station Yard. The swimming pool is just opposite. There is also a sports ground, but that is a ten-minute walk beyond the pool, so the trust has not added a stop there.

The last stop, and the end of the line, is Saint Anne's Square in the town centre. The library is on the north side of the square, and many of the town's best shops are within five minutes on foot. You may be wondering about the primary school. It has its own minibus for pupils, so there is no stop for it.

I spoke to one resident, a retired teacher called Margaret, who has lived in Harlow Green for forty years. She told me that for the last six years she has depended on her daughter to drive her to the shops, and that the new bus will give her back her independence. Stories like hers are why the trust has worked so hard.

The trust also plans to publish a printed timetable that will be delivered to every house along the route, and a copy will be pinned up in the post office, the library and the doctors' waiting room. There will also be a free phone number and a simple website, for anyone who prefers to plan a journey in advance.
To celebrate the launch, all journeys on the first Monday will be free. The trust will also hand out a short survey, and it would love to hear what you think, so please fill it in.
That's all on the bus for now. After the break, we'll hear from a local beekeeper who says this summer has been the strangest in years.

listening.title: Designing a plant-growth experiment
listening.titleVi: Thiết kế thí nghiệm về sự phát triển của cây trồng
listening.context: Two biology students discuss the design of an experiment on lettuce seedlings with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Zoe and Marcus, discussing the design of an experiment with their tutor, Dr Fenwick. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Come in, both of you. I've read your draft plan for the plant experiment. Tell me how you reached your decisions, starting with the choice of plant.
At first I wanted to use bean plants, because there is a lot of research on them. But beans take about six weeks to flower, and we only have a short time.
So we switched to lettuce. The seeds are cheap, and we can get them from the university shop, but the main reason is how fast they grow.

Good. You can see clear differences between lettuce seedlings within a couple of weeks. Now, you want to compare three colours of light, red, blue and white. How many seedlings did you plan for each colour?
Five. We thought that would be easier to manage in one growth room.
I'm afraid five is too few. If one seedling grows badly for some reason, it distorts the whole average. Ten per colour should be enough for a student project.
Twenty would be even better, wouldn't it?
It would, but you don't have the tray space. Ten is a sensible compromise. That makes thirty seedlings altogether.
OK. Ten each, then. Next, we were going to measure the height of each seedling with a ruler every week.
Hmm. Height can be misleading with lettuce, because it spreads its leaves outwards rather than growing upwards.
Would leaf area be better? We could photograph the plants and use software to calculate it.

You could, but you would need to calibrate the camera and the software, and that takes time. A better measure is dry mass at the end of the experiment. You harvest the plants, dry them in the oven for two days and weigh them.
That sounds simpler. We'll do that.
And how long will the experiment last? I would like to see four weeks.
The trouble is that the growth room is only available to us for three weeks. Another group needs it after that.
That's a shame. Then three weeks it will have to be. Start on a Monday so that the harvest falls on a weekday.
Before we go on, remind me of your hypothesis. What do you actually expect to find?
We think the seedlings under red and blue light will grow better than those under white light, because plants absorb those two colours most strongly.
Although, to be honest, I think the differences may turn out to be small. Some of the articles we read were not very clear about it.

That is perfectly acceptable. A good experiment can show that there is no difference, and that is still a result. What matters is that your method is fair and that you can explain exactly what you did, so that someone else could repeat it.
Should we also write down how the seedlings look, for example if the leaves are pale or yellow?
Yes, keep a short diary with photographs once a week. It will not be part of your main data, but it often helps you to explain a surprising result when you write the discussion.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, I can see two practical problems with your plan. The first is the position of the lamp racks. You've put one beside the window and one beside the radiator, so those plants will be at different temperatures.
We hadn't thought of that. We were only worried about the colour of the light.

That is exactly the trouble. The temperature must be the same for every group. The second problem is the watering. Your plan says each plant gets a splash of water when it looks dry. That is far too uneven, because a splash from one of you will not be the same as a splash from the other.
So we should measure it out?

Yes, fifty millilitres per tray, at the same time each day. Don't worry about the other things you listed. All the seeds come from one packet, so that is fine, and the department will supply the lamps, so cost is not an issue. The LED lamps stay cool, so brightness will not harm the seedlings either.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: So what equipment should we book from the lab?
First, a light meter. You need to check that each lamp gives the same level of brightness at the height of the plants, because lamps of different colours can look very different.
And something to record the temperature. Could we just look at a thermometer each morning?
A data logger would be better. It takes a reading every hour, and it would also have shown you the effect of the radiator. Borrow one from the technician.
What about the length of the day? Do we need to switch the lamps on and off ourselves?
Certainly not. Plug them into a timer switch so that they stay on for exactly sixteen hours a day. If you switch them on by hand, you are bound to forget one day.
And the digital balance is for weighing the plants at the end?
Yes. Use the one that measures to two decimal places, because the dried seedlings will weigh very little.
Great. I'll book everything this afternoon. Thank you, Dr Fenwick.
One more question. When we analyse the results, should we use a statistical test, or just compare the averages?

Compare the averages first and draw a simple bar chart with error bars. Then use a one-way analysis of variance to see whether the differences are real. I will show you how in next week's workshop, so do not worry if you have not used it before.
That's a relief. I was afraid we would have to learn a whole new program by ourselves.

You will manage. Many students find that the planning is harder than the analysis, and you have already done the difficult part today. Remember to keep a copy of your raw data in two places, in case a computer fails during the last week.
Send me the corrected plan by Friday, and then you can start sowing the seeds on Monday.

items.q: Why did the students choose lettuce for their experiment?
options: There is a lot of research on it.

listening.title: A short history of bridge engineering
listening.titleVi: Lược sử kỹ thuật xây cầu
listening.context: A lecturer in civil engineering describes how bridge design developed from simple crossings to modern structures.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the history of bridge engineering. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning, everyone. Today's lecture is a short history of bridge engineering. I'll try to show that almost every great step forward came from learning a lesson, often a painful one, about materials and forces.

Let's begin at the very beginning. The first bridges were not designed at all. People used what nature gave them: a fallen tree trunk across a stream, or a line of flat stones that could be stepped on.

Some of these simple crossings survive. In parts of Britain you can still see clapper bridges, which are flat stone slabs resting on piles of rocks. They work for short distances, but a slab that is too long will simply crack under its own weight.
The big change came with the Romans, who understood something that earlier builders had missed: the arch, which pushes the weight outwards and down into the supports.
Stone is very strong when it is squeezed, and in an arch every stone is squeezed by its neighbours. That is why many Roman bridges are still standing after nearly two thousand years.

The Romans also had a second advantage, which was a better building material. They mixed volcanic ash with lime to make a concrete that could set underwater, and that allowed them to build strong foundations in the middle of a river.

After the Roman Empire declined, bridge building in Europe slowed down, but it never stopped. In the Middle Ages, towns were proud of their stone bridges, and the bridges were often very busy places in their own right.
Many medieval bridges carried rows of shops, and the rent from the shops paid for the repair of the bridge. It was an early example of a structure that paid for its own maintenance.
However, medieval arches were narrow, and the piers in the river blocked the flow of water, which made floods worse. Some bridges were damaged every winter, which was an expensive problem.

Bridge builders in other parts of the world were meanwhile finding their own solutions. In mountain regions, people wove ropes from grass and vines and hung them across deep valleys, and some of these rope bridges were renewed by whole villages every year. The skill lay not in the materials but in the organisation, because the work had to be shared out and finished before the rainy season.

In some parts of Asia, builders also developed bridges with a roof over the walkway. The roof was not just for comfort. It protected the timber from rain and sun, and so doubled the life of the bridge. It is a good reminder that maintenance has always been as important as clever design.
The next revolution came with the Industrial Revolution and a new material, iron. The first large bridge in the world made of cast iron was completed in seventeen seventy-nine.
It looked very different from a stone bridge. Because iron is much stronger than stone for its weight, the builders could make the arch lighter and the opening between the supports much wider.

Yet cast iron has a serious weakness. It resists being pushed or squeezed very well, but it is poor under tension, which means when it is pulled or stretched. A cast iron beam can fail suddenly and without warning, and several early iron bridges collapsed for that reason.

Engineers therefore turned to steel in the nineteenth century. Steel was more expensive at first, and it was not cheaper to produce until later in the century, but it solved the main problem, because it is far stronger under tension than iron.

I should add that steel does not rust any less than iron, so painting and maintenance remained an endless job. A famous bridge in Scotland, for example, has a team of painters who are said to start again as soon as they finish.
Now, one disaster in particular changed the thinking of engineers. In eighteen seventy-nine, a long railway bridge collapsed in a storm while a train was crossing it. Many people died.

The investigation showed that the designers had not taken proper account of wind pressure. After that, engineers began calculating the force of the wind on every large bridge, and the rules they introduced are still used today.

That brings me to suspension bridges, where the road hangs from cables slung between tall towers. Their great advantage is that they can span very wide gaps, sometimes more than a kilometre, with only two towers and nothing at all standing in the water.
People often assume suspension bridges are cheaper, but that isn't true. The anchors that hold the cables at each end are enormous, and they cost a great deal.

Beyond the towers and cables, there is the question of how a bridge behaves in everyday use. A large bridge is never still. It expands in summer heat and shrinks in winter cold, so designers include special joints that allow the deck to move by several centimetres without damage. Engineers also fit sensors that report on vibration and movement, so that a problem can be noticed long before it becomes dangerous.

Finally, how do engineers check a modern design? In the past they often built small models and tested them in wind tunnels. Today most of the testing is done on computers, which can simulate the wind, the traffic and even an earthquake before any steel is ordered.
A wind tunnel is now used only for a final check on the biggest and most unusual designs. Full-size prototypes are almost never built, because they would cost too much.

There is one more point worth making about the people behind the bridges. For most of history, bridge builders were not scientists. They were masons and carpenters who passed their skills from master to apprentice, and who learned by watching what stood and what fell. Mathematics only became a real tool for bridge design in the eighteenth century, when engineers began to calculate how much load a beam could carry before it bent.

That change matters because it made bridges more daring. Once designers could predict the behaviour of a structure on paper, they dared to build longer, lighter and more elegant bridges than any craftsman would have attempted by instinct alone. But it also meant that mistakes in the calculations could be disastrous, which is why modern engineers are required to have their designs checked independently by a second team.

To sum up, the history of bridges is a history of learning from failure, and every generation of engineers has built on the lessons of the last. Next week we'll look at tunnels, which present quite different problems.
