listening.title: Getting a car insurance quote
listening.titleVi: Xin báo giá bảo hiểm xe hơi qua điện thoại
listening.context: A woman phones an insurance company to ask for a quote for car insurance.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning an insurance company to ask for a quote for her car. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good afternoon, Redstone Direct, Gareth speaking. How can I help you?
Hi, Gareth. I'd like a quote for car insurance, please. My current policy runs out at the end of next month, and I'd like to compare prices before I renew it.
Of course. It only takes about ten minutes, and I'll enter your details as we go along. Could I have your full name, please?
Yes, it's Leanne Pemberton.
Could you spell the surname for me?
P, E, M, B, E, R, T, O, N.
Thank you. And what's the registration number of the car?
K, L, one, nine, R, Z, P.
Lovely, I've got that. And what sort of car is it? A saloon, a hatchback, a four-by-four?
It's a Navaro Trek. People often think it's a hatchback because of the way the back slopes, but on the registration document it's classed as an estate.
Right, an estate. That can make a small difference to the price, so it's good to be exact. And what year was it made?
I bought it in twenty nineteen, but it was second-hand even then. It was actually built two years earlier, in 2017.
OK, so the year of manufacture is 2017. Now, do you use the car for work?
Only for getting to my office and back. I never drive during the working day.
So that's social use plus commuting. Roughly how many miles do you drive in a year?
I used to do about twelve thousand, but since last spring I've been working from home three days a week, so it's much less now. Eight thousand is more like it.
I'll put down eight thousand miles. Do try to be accurate, because if you drive a lot more than you declare, the company could refuse a claim.
Yes, eight thousand is about right.
And where is the car kept overnight? In a garage, on the street, or somewhere else?
We don't have a garage. It used to be parked on the road outside the house, but last year we paved over the front garden, so now it stays on the driveway.
That's better for the price, because a car on a driveway is less likely to be damaged or stolen. How many years of no-claims discount do you have?
Five years. I haven't made a claim since I passed my test.
Will anyone else be driving the car regularly? A husband, a partner, a grown-up child, perhaps?
Just my husband, occasionally, when we go away for the weekend. He's been driving for twenty years and he has a clean licence.
Then I'll add him as a named driver. Excellent. Any accidents or driving convictions in the last five years?
None at all. I did have a parking fine once, but that isn't a driving offence.
No, that doesn't count. Thank you, that's all the information I need for the form.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: So, what sort of price am I looking at?
I've found a comprehensive policy for you. If you pay for the whole year in one go, the price is four hundred and eighty-six pounds.
And what if I pay monthly? I'd find that easier at the moment.
That would be twelve payments of forty-three pounds fifty, which comes to five hundred and twenty-two pounds altogether, because interest is added. So paying annually is the cheaper option.
I see. I'll think about it. What's the excess on the policy?

As standard it's two hundred pounds, which is the amount you pay towards any claim. You can choose a higher voluntary excess to bring the price down, but I'd leave it as it is, because the saving is only about fifteen pounds.
That seems sensible. Are there any extras I should consider?
Quite a few. A courtesy car while yours is being repaired is a popular one.
I already get a courtesy car through my bank account, so I won't need that. But I don't have anything in case the car breaks down.
Then I'd recommend breakdown cover. It would add about thirty-four pounds to the price, and it includes help at home as well as on the road.
I'll certainly think about that one. How long does this quote last?
The quote is guaranteed for thirty days, so you have plenty of time to compare. There's also a ten per cent discount for anyone who buys within fourteen days, but you don't have to decide today.
That's very helpful, Gareth. Could you send it all to me in writing?
Of course. I'll email the quote and a reference number this afternoon. If you ring back, just give the reference and anyone here will be able to find your details.
Perfect. Thank you for your time.
You're welcome, Leanne. Enjoy the rest of your day.

listening.title: A wetland visitor centre
listening.titleVi: Giới thiệu trung tâm đón khách vùng đầm lầy
listening.context: A ranger welcomes a group of visitors and describes a wetland reserve and its visitor centre.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a ranger welcoming visitors to a wetland reserve. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to Saltmere Marsh. My name is Marian, and I'm one of the rangers here. Before you set off on your walk, I'd like to tell you a little about the place and how to get the most out of your visit.

Many people are surprised to hear that this wetland is not completely natural. Forty years ago, this whole area was a gravel quarry. When the digging stopped, the pits slowly filled with water, and the reserve was created by flooding them deliberately and planting reeds around the edges. Before that, some people had suggested building a reservoir here, but the idea was dropped.

Today the reserve covers about two hundred hectares, and more than two hundred species of bird have been recorded here. When is the best time to come? Spring is lovely, with the reeds turning green and the first dragonflies appearing, and in summer there are plenty of young birds. But if you really want to see large numbers, October is the month, because that is when the wintering flocks arrive from the north, and thousands of geese and ducks gather on the main lake.

Now a word about the paths. We have three main trails, and the shortest, which is the boardwalk, is ideal if you have young children with you. It is flat and fenced, it takes about forty minutes, and there are interesting things to see all the way along. The longer marsh trail is lovely, but it can be muddy, and small children tend to get tired halfway round.

I'd like to explain the biggest problem we face. You might expect me to say litter, or visitors leaving the paths, and of course those are things we ask you to think about. But the real threat is a plant. Floating pennywort was brought here from another country as a decoration for garden ponds, and it grows so fast that it can cover a whole pool in a few weeks, blocking out the light and killing the native plants underneath. Our staff spend a large part of the summer pulling it out by hand.

Whatever time of year you visit, please dress for the weather. It is often windier out on the reeds than you would expect, and the paths can be wet even after a dry week, so waterproof shoes are a good idea. In winter the main lake can look beautiful in the early morning mist, but it is also very cold, and we keep a few spare hats and gloves in the shop for anyone who has come unprepared.

That brings me to our volunteers, who are the heart of the reserve. The bird counts are carried out by a small team who have all been trained, and the paths are repaired by a local contractor, so we don't need help with either of those. What we are always short of is volunteers to lead guided tours for school groups and visitors, so if you enjoy talking to people, do ask at the desk.

The visitor centre itself is open from nine to five every day except Christmas Day. You'll find the cafe, the shop and the toilets here, and there's a small exhibition about how the quarry became a marsh. Entry to the reserve is free, though we are grateful for donations.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me tell you about the places you can visit, and what you will find at each of them. You can follow them on the map in your leaflet.

Your first stop is the Reed Walk, which starts just behind the visitor centre. Halfway along there's a raised viewing platform with a gentle ramp, so wheelchair users and anyone with limited mobility can look out across the reedbeds. Many people say the view from there is the best in the reserve.

If you carry on to the south, you'll reach Dragonfly Pond. This is the place for families. There is a wooden platform at the water's edge, where we lend out nets and trays, and children can try pond-dipping and find out what lives under the water. Please remember to put everything back in the pond afterwards.

The path then bends round to Heron Hide, which is the largest of our hides. You can see most of the main lake from its windows, and a set of telescopes is available there, free of charge, so you don't need to bring your own binoculars. It does get busy at weekends, so the early morning is a good time to go.

After that, a short walk along East Dyke will bring you to a sheltered spot with several picnic tables. If you have brought lunch with you, that's the place to eat it. I should say that we don't have a playground anywhere on the reserve, because we want to keep the wildlife as undisturbed as possible.

Finally, the path ends at the Old Quay, where our small electric boats leave on the hour in summer. The trip lasts forty minutes, and a guide explains what you can see from the water. Booking is advised, and you can do that at the visitor centre desk before you set out.

A few last things. Please keep dogs on a short lead, because ground-nesting birds are easily frightened, and please don't feed the ducks, because bread is bad for them. If you see anything unusual, such as an injured bird, please tell a member of staff rather than trying to help it yourself. We also run a children's activity morning every Saturday, which is a very popular event.
Thank you for listening. Enjoy your walk, and I hope you see something special today.

listening.title: Designing a survey on daily travel
listening.titleVi: Thiết kế bảng hỏi khảo sát việc đi lại hằng ngày
listening.context: Two students discuss the draft of a questionnaire about daily commuting with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Ines and Rory, discussing a questionnaire about daily commuting with their tutor, Dr Mensah. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Hello, both. I've had a look at your draft questionnaire on how people get to work and to the university. Let's start with your sample. You were going to survey students only, weren't you?
Yes, originally. Students are easy to reach, and we have access to the mailing lists for all the departments.
But we've been wondering about including staff as well, because most of the students we know live quite close to the campus.

I think that is a good instinct. If you only ask students, you will probably find that most of them walk or cycle for ten or fifteen minutes. Staff often live much further away, so you will get a far wider range of journey lengths, and that will make your analysis more interesting.
That's what we hoped. We also thought about printing the questionnaires and handing them out at the entrance.

You could, but an online form is better here. People can fill it in on the train or at home, and you don't have to type the answers in by hand. Just make sure you test the link on a phone, because many people will open it there.

Dr Mensah, we put in a section about how stressful the journey is, with a scale from one to ten. Ines loves it, but I'm honestly not convinced. I can't see how anyone can turn something like stress into a number.

That's a fair reservation, and people have argued about it in the research literature. But I would keep it. It is a self-reported rating, and as long as you describe it as that, it can still show you which kinds of journey people dislike most. Reporting a feeling is not the same as measuring it exactly.
Good, then I win that argument.
Only if the results are interesting, Ines.

Now let me turn to individual questions. Your first question asks, how long is your daily commute? Think about the person reading that. Does it mean one way, or there and back? Some people will answer fifteen and others will answer thirty, when they actually travel for the same time.
Oh, I see. We should say one way, or ask for the time in each direction.

Yes, that would solve it. Overall, the draft is thorough, perhaps a little too thorough. Twenty-six questions is a lot for an online form, and respondents tend to give up around the twentieth. I would aim to cut it by four or five.
We can combine a couple of the questions about parking.
And we could drop the question about what time people leave home. Nobody will remember it exactly, and it doesn't really tell us anything about the journey.

I agree. A few questions in a survey are there because someone thought they might be useful one day. Ask yourselves of each one, what will I do with the answer? If you can't say, delete it. That also helps with the number of replies, because a shorter form usually brings a much better response.
How many replies should we aim for, realistically?
For a project of this size, about a hundred and fifty completed forms would give you something worth analysing. Many students are disappointed to get twenty, so send a reminder after one week.
Good idea, we'll send a reminder.
Thank you. Before you go any further, though, I want you to think about two things that must happen before the main survey.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: First, run a pilot. Ask ten people, friends or relatives who are not in your sample, to complete the questionnaire and tell you what confused them. You will always find something that you had not noticed, because you have read the questions so many times yourselves. Second, you need ethical approval, because you will be collecting personal information. The form is on the department website, and the committee meets every second Thursday, so you should submit it soon.
Should we offer a prize draw to get more people to reply?

That is optional, and I don't think it is necessary for a student project. It can even attract people who rush through the answers just to enter. And you don't need a statistician to check the questionnaire either. I'm happy to look at it myself once you have the revised version.
OK. A pilot and the ethics form. We'll do both this week.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Now I'd like to go through a few of the individual questions, because several of them could be improved. Your question about which means of transport people use most often gives them a list: car, bus, train, bicycle and walking. But someone might travel by motorbike, or by scooter, or by ferry.
So we should add another category, where they can write in their own answer?

Exactly. Then you won't force people to choose something that isn't true. Next, you ask people for their exact age. Most people are happy to give it, but there is really no need for that level of detail. Offer age bands, such as eighteen to twenty-four, twenty-five to thirty-four, and so on. It is quicker to answer, and it feels less personal.
Fine. Another one that bothered me was the question, how satisfied are you with the bus service and how reliable do you find it?

You've noticed the problem yourself. That is two questions in one. Someone could be very satisfied with the frequency of buses but unhappy with how often they arrive late, and they would not know which to answer. Split it into two separate questions.
That makes sense. And the question about household income? We put it near the start.

That is the one I would move. People are sensitive about money, and if they see it in the first few lines, some of them will close the page. Put it at the very end, when they have already put in some effort and feel more committed.
I'd never have thought about the order of the questions mattering so much.

It matters a great deal. Many students find that the writing of the questions is harder than the analysis of the results. If you want, send me the revised draft by Monday, and I'll give you comments by Wednesday.
Brilliant. Thank you, Dr Mensah.

listening.title: Seed banks and crop diversity
listening.titleVi: Ngân hàng hạt giống và sự đa dạng cây trồng
listening.context: A lecturer in agricultural science explains why seed banks exist and how they store and use the seeds of food crops.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on seed banks and crop diversity. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning. Today I want to talk about a part of agriculture that most people never see: the seed bank. It sounds like a rather dull warehouse, but I hope to persuade you that it is one of the most important insurance policies we have for feeding the world.

Let me begin with the problem it was invented to solve. For about ten thousand years, farmers saved seed from their best plants and sowed it the following year. Over time, each valley and each village ended up with its own varieties, adapted to local soil, weather and taste. Then, in the twentieth century, farming changed. Governments and companies promoted a small number of modern varieties that gave very high yields, and farmers in many countries abandoned their old ones, because the new seed simply made more money.

That was good for harvests in the short term, but it created a danger. If every field in a region contains plants that are genetically identical, then a single disease or pest that can attack one plant can attack them all. History has plenty of examples, and the worst of them led to famine. Once the old varieties have disappeared from the fields, they are gone for ever, along with whatever useful characteristics they carried. Scientists became alarmed in the middle of the last century, and that is when the first serious collections were started.

So how do you keep a seed alive for decades? The answer is to make it believe that nothing is happening. A seed is a living thing, but it can be put into a kind of deep sleep if it is kept dry and cold.

The first step is drying. Seeds that go into a bank are dried carefully until water makes up only about five per cent of their weight. Any more than that and the seeds may rot, or mould may grow on them, or ice crystals may form inside them and destroy them when they are frozen. Seeds are then sealed in airtight foil packets, which keep out moisture from the air.

The second step is cold. Most large banks keep their long-term collections in a vault at minus eighteen degrees Celsius, which is roughly the temperature of an ordinary domestic freezer. At that temperature, the chemical processes that age a seed slow down enormously. Some kinds of seed can survive for centuries in such conditions, although many banks prefer not to promise more than a few decades.

But what if the bank itself is destroyed by a flood, a fire, a war or even an electricity failure? To guard against that, important collections are copied, and the duplicates are sent to a remote vault tunnelled deep into a mountain, in a cold northern region. The owners of the original samples keep ownership, and they are the only people who can ask for them back. It works rather like a safe deposit box in a bank, except that what is inside is the future of our food.

Now, a seed bank is not a museum. Seeds that are never tested are of little use, because nobody knows whether they are still alive. Each sample is therefore checked at regular intervals, typically once a decade. A small number of seeds are taken out, planted on damp paper or in soil, and counted to see how many sprout. If the proportion falls below a threshold, usually around eighty-five per cent, the bank has to take action.

That action is called regeneration. Technicians sow what is left of the sample, look after the plants, and harvest fresh seed. It is a slow and expensive job, and it needs great care. If the plants are not kept apart from others of the same species, pollen from a different variety can blow in and alter the genetic makeup of the sample. The bank would then be storing something slightly different from what it was given, which would defeat the whole purpose.

Not every seed can be stored in this way. Most of our familiar cereals and vegetables produce seeds that tolerate drying and freezing without any harm. But the seeds of many tropical trees do not. Cocoa is the best-known example, and many palms are the same. If these seeds are dried, they die. For such species, scientists must use other methods, such as keeping tiny pieces of tissue in liquid nitrogen, or growing living plants in a field collection. Both are far more costly than a freezer, and it remains an unresolved problem.

Why does all this matter in practice? There are two main reasons. The first concerns the kind of plants farmers themselves developed. Traditional varieties that have been shaped over many generations by farmers in a single region are known as landraces. They are often less productive than modern crops, but they are tough, and they may carry resistance to local diseases or tolerate poor soil. Holding them in a bank means that those qualities are not lost when the last farmer who grew them retires.

The second reason is plant breeding. Breeders are constantly looking for new characteristics to put into the crops we eat, and the climate is changing faster than the plants can adapt on their own. Breeders have already used stored seeds to find genes that help crops cope with long periods without rain, and drought-resistant varieties of several staple foods now exist because somebody took the trouble to preserve an obscure seed from a dry region.

I should be honest and say that banks cannot do everything. A seed in a freezer cannot adapt to a warmer world, because it is not growing. And a packet of seed does not carry the knowledge of the people who grew it: when to plant, how to cook it, which animals to keep it away from. Some scientists therefore argue that seed banks should work alongside what is grown in real fields, rather than replace it.

That argument has encouraged a different kind of seed collection, one run by ordinary people. In many towns there are now community seed libraries, which are usually kept in a cabinet in a public library or a community centre. Gardeners borrow packets of seed free of charge and plant them, and when the harvest is over they are asked to return some of the seed they have collected. It is a small-scale system, but it keeps varieties alive in use, and it spreads knowledge as well as seed.

There is also a question of fairness. Many of the plants in the great collections were originally gathered from the fields of poorer countries, and those countries have argued that they should share the benefits when companies develop a profitable new variety from their material. International agreements now try to address that, although negotiations about the details have been long and sometimes bitter.

To sum up, a seed bank rests on three simple ideas: keep the seed dry, keep it cold, and keep a copy somewhere safe. Around those ideas, however, lies a great deal of careful testing, regular renewal and careful bargaining between nations. Next week, we will look at what happens after the seeds leave the vault, and how breeders turn an obscure plant into the wheat on your table.

listening.title: Booking a stall at a craft fair
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký gian hàng tại hội chợ thủ công
listening.context: A man phones the organiser of a craft fair to book a stall for his candle-making business.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning the organiser of a craft fair to book a stall. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good morning, Eastvale Craft Fair office. This is Nadia.
Hello, Nadia. My name is Callum Brennick, and I'd like to book a stall at this year's winter fair, if there is still space.
There is, but it's filling up quickly. I'll complete the application form as we talk. Could you spell your surname for me, please?
Yes, it's B, R, E, N, N, I, C, K.
Thank you. And what's the name of your business?
Bluebird Candles. I run it from my garage at home, and this will be my first time at a fair of this size, so I'm a little nervous.
Don't be. Most of our traders started small. What's the best number to reach you on?
My mobile is oh seven eight nine six, double two one, double four seven.
Oh seven eight nine six, double two one, double four seven. Lovely. Now, what will you be selling? Our application form asks us to record the main product.
Last year I sold soap as well, but I've stopped making it because it took too much time. So this year it's handmade candles, and nothing else.

Candles are always popular at the winter fair. Now, about the size of your stall. We have a standard stall, which is three metres wide, and a double stall, which is six metres wide. There is nothing in between.
I was hoping for four metres, but I suppose that's not possible. I have a lot of stock and a display shelf, so the double stall sounds better. Six metres, please.

Six metres it is. We have two halls this year. The Harcourt Hall is for food and drink, and the Tamarind Hall is for crafts and gifts. As you make candles, you would be in the Tamarind Hall. That's T, A, M, A, R, I, N, D.
Thank you. I think I'll be in good company there.
You will. Do you need electricity at the stall? Some traders want lights or a card reader, and we include sockets in the price.
I'll need one for the lights, so one socket. Actually, I'll probably bring a card reader as well, so I'd better ask for two.
Two sockets, noted.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: What does the double stall cost?
The standard stall is a hundred and forty pounds for the whole weekend. The double stall is two hundred and forty, which is a little less than twice as much, so it is good value.
That's reasonable. Does that include a table?
I'm afraid not. You can bring your own, or hire tables from us at fifteen pounds each. Chairs are free, and we provide a banner with your business name.
I'll bring my own tables. When can I set up my stall?

Traders can enter the hall from half past seven on Saturday morning, and the doors open to the public at ten. Most people need at least an hour and a half to arrange everything, so please don't leave it late.
Understood. Half past seven it is. Is there anything to pay in advance?

Yes, we ask for a deposit to hold the space. For food traders it is fifty percent, because of the extra checks we have to carry out, but for craft stalls it is thirty percent of the stall fee, payable within a week.
That's fine. I can pay by card now, if you like.
Better to wait until you have the confirmation email, which I'll send this afternoon. It will include a plan of the hall and a parking pass for your van.
Wonderful. And if I have to cancel, is there a charge?
You can cancel without charge up to a month before the fair, and after that we keep the deposit. Most traders never need to.
One more thing. Will there be much advertising for the fair? I'm hoping to attract customers who have never heard of my business.

Yes, we put posters in every library and café in the area, and there are adverts on local radio for the two weeks before. We also post a profile of each trader on our website, so please send me a short description of your business and two photographs of your candles by the end of next week.
I'll do that tonight. Should I mention that the candles are made from natural wax?

Definitely. Customers like to know how things are made, and it gives you something to talk about at the stall. Many of our visitors come back every year, and they enjoy meeting the people behind the products.
Good to know. Thank you very much, Nadia. I'm looking forward to it.
You're welcome, Callum. Welcome to the fair, and good luck with the candles.

listening.title: A welcome to the farmers market
listening.titleVi: Giới thiệu chợ nông sản địa phương cho cư dân mới
listening.context: The manager of a local farmers market explains how the market works to people who have recently moved to the town.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the manager of a farmers market talking to people who have recently moved to the town. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to this short orientation session for new residents. I'm Ingrid Haldane, and I manage the Eastbrook Farmers Market, which many of you will have noticed on your way here. I'd like to explain how it works, so that you can get the most out of it from your very first visit.

First, a little history. The market began twelve years ago with just eight stalls in the old square beside the church. It grew quickly, and by last year we had forty producers asking for a pitch, but the square could only hold fifteen of them. Nobody ever complained about flooding, and the council had no plans to rebuild the square. We simply ran out of room. So two years ago we moved to the car park behind the library, which can take up to sixty stalls.

The market is open every Saturday from eight until one, and on the first Sunday of each month we hold a special market with craft stalls as well as food. People often ask me who is allowed to sell. You might imagine that every trader must be a farmer, but that isn't so. We welcome bakers, cheesemakers and people who make jam, as long as everything they sell is grown or made within thirty miles of the town. Anything brought in from further away, such as imported fruit, is not allowed, and we check this with a visit to every producer once a year.

Now, a tip about timing. If you want the best choice, come before nine. By ten, the most popular bread and the freshest vegetables have often gone. You may be tempted to wait until the end, because some traders reduce their prices in the last half hour, but the choice is poor by then, and I wouldn't recommend it unless you are very flexible about what you buy. Around eleven it gets extremely crowded, with long queues at the coffee stall, so that is the worst time for a quiet visit with a pushchair.

Payment is the next thing to explain. Cash is welcome, and a few stalls take cards, but the mobile signal in the car park is weak, and the card machines often fail. So we introduced market tokens. You can buy them at the information tent by the entrance, and every stall accepts them. Each token is worth one pound, and you can exchange any that you don't spend before closing time, so there is no risk.

I'm often asked what I am proudest of. The number of visitors has doubled since the move, and we now welcome around three thousand people each Saturday. We also keep our prices among the lowest in the region. But what I'm most proud of is our school gardening club. Last spring about thirty children grew vegetables in raised beds beside the market and sold them on a stall of their own, and they raised enough money to buy tools for their school. For me, that is what a market should do.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me introduce five of the stalls that you will find, in the order that you meet them as you walk in from the entrance. The first is Hillside Bakery, on your left. Their sourdough is excellent, but it is baked in small batches, and it sells out before ten almost every week. If you want a loaf, please don't arrive late.

Next is Mossgate Dairy, which makes cheese from its own herd of goats and cows. They always have a table of small pieces for you to try, and nobody pushes you to buy anything, so it's a good place to learn what you like.

Third, there is the honey stall run by the Bramble family. They don't offer tastings, for hygiene reasons, but you can order larger jars in advance and collect them the next Saturday. That's very useful before Christmas, when they often run out of stock.

The fourth stall sells fish. The fresh fish comes from the coast, which is almost eighty miles away, so the van can make the trip only once a month, on the first Saturday. If you see it, buy it, and if you miss it, you will have to wait.

The last is Old Orchard Preserves, at the far end of the car park. It's a jam and chutney stall that changed hands in the spring, when the original owners retired and a young couple took over. They kept the old recipes but have added some new flavours, so it's worth another look if you tried it years ago.

A few practical points before I finish. Please bring your own bags, because we no longer provide plastic ones, and many traders will give you a small discount if you bring back a clean egg box or jam jar. Dogs are welcome as long as they are kept on a lead, but the cheese and fish stalls ask that they are not brought close to the counter.

If you would like to help, we are always looking for volunteers to put up the stalls at seven in the morning, and to collect the leftover vegetables at closing time. That food goes to the local food bank, and nothing is wasted. You can sign up at the information tent, or you can write your name on the list by the door today.

Please also take a look at the map on the wall behind me, which shows where each stall stands, and the leaflet beside it, which lists every producer, what they sell and which days they attend. Finally, you can find a weekly newsletter on our noticeboard and at the library, telling you which producers are coming and what is in season. Thank you for listening, and I hope to see you all on Saturday.

listening.title: A business case study on a bakery chain
listening.titleVi: Phân tích tình huống kinh doanh về chuỗi tiệm bánh
listening.context: Two business students discuss their case study on an expanding chain of bakeries with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Priya and Tomas, discussing a business case study with their tutor, Dr Lindqvist. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Right, let's make a start. I've been through your plan for the Crumb Lane Bakeries case study, and I have a few questions. First of all, what made you choose that company?
Mainly because the owner is facing an interesting decision. The company has six shops, and she has to choose between opening more of her own or selling franchises to other people.

That was the deciding factor for me, too. We looked at a pizza chain as well, but it only had one realistic option, so there was nothing to compare. This one lets us argue both sides. Mind you, none of us has any connection to the firm, and the financial figures took ages to find.
Good. A case with a real choice makes for a stronger report. Now, your plan is to recommend opening ten new shops in a single year. What was your reasoning?
The company has grown by about five shops every two years, and the owner thinks that moving faster would let her take the best sites before her competitors do.

I'm not convinced. Their cash reserves are modest, and ten leases at once would mean a great deal of money going out before any comes in. If a few of the new shops were slow to attract customers, the whole company could be in serious trouble. I'd suggest three or four, at most.
I see what you mean. We hadn't really looked at the cash flow in that much detail.
Then it needs looking at. What about the franchise option? Tomas, what do you think?

Honestly, I keep going back and forth. Franchising works well for famous brands, but I'm not sure a regional firm with six shops has a name strong enough for people to pay for. Priya is more positive than I am.
I think it could work if the owner chose the franchisees carefully. But I agree that we need some evidence from other small companies.
Both views are reasonable, as long as you support them. Now, you also carried out a customer survey. Tell me about it.
We asked a hundred and twenty customers as they left two of the shops. Most of them said they would happily buy from a new branch near their home.

Be careful there. Those respondents are people who already buy from the company. They tell you very little about residents in a town where nobody has heard of Crumb Lane. So I'd treat the results as encouraging, and not as proof.
That's a fair point. We'll say so in the report.

Good. That kind of honesty about your own evidence is what earns the higher marks. Examiners are not looking for a perfect answer to the owner's problem, because there isn't one. They are looking for a clear argument that shows you understand the risks as well as the benefits, and that you can explain why you rejected the alternatives.
That's a relief, because I was worried that we might be marked down if our recommendation turned out to be wrong.

Not at all. A cautious recommendation backed by sound reasoning will always score better than a bold one that ignores the numbers. Many students feel they have to be dramatic, and I find that the quieter, more careful reports are usually the most convincing.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, in your risks section you listed five possible problems. I'd like you to choose the two that matter most, because a presentation can't cover everything. What do you think?
Rising flour prices is one that we mentioned, but the company has a fixed-price contract with its supplier for the next two years.
Then it isn't urgent. What about the supermarkets?

They already sell cheap bread, but people come to Crumb Lane for fresh pastries and cakes, so I'd leave that out. What worries me more is keeping every loaf the same. At the moment the head baker checks the products herself, and with more shops that would be impossible.
That is a crucial point for any brand. Customers expect the same taste in every shop. Anything else?
Yes, finding enough skilled bakers. Training a new one takes about two years, and the company is already short of experienced staff.
And the high rents in busy streets are a problem too, but we already deal with that in the finance section.
Exactly, so there's no need to repeat it. Then I think you have your two main risks.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Dr Lindqvist, we've been thinking about how to organise the presentation. It has four sections, and we're not sure how to handle each one.

Let's take them in turn. Start with the market analysis. Your numbers are fine, but a list of percentages can be dull. Pick out a few comments from the survey and quote the customers directly. That brings the figures to life.
OK. What about the financial forecast? We only have one set of figures.
That's a weakness. Add a worst-case scenario, in which sales are twenty percent lower than expected. If the plan still survives that, your audience will trust it far more.
I was thinking of inviting a manager from the company to speak about the operations section.

That's kind, but it isn't necessary, and it would use up some of your time. Instead, draw a flow chart showing how the dough is made at the central kitchen and delivered to the shops each morning. A diagram is easier to follow than a paragraph.
And the conclusion?
Keep it short. No more than two slides, with your recommendation stated clearly on the second one. People remember the last thing they see.
That's very helpful. When do you need the revised outline?

By Friday at noon. Then we can meet briefly on Monday to go through the slides, and you will have a week to practise before the actual presentation. Don't forget that the whole thing must last no more than fifteen minutes, including questions.
Fifteen minutes is quite short. We'd better start practising early.

Yes, and time yourselves. Most students run over, and the marks for delivery depend a lot on keeping to the limit. Ask a friend to hold a stopwatch, and stop at the exact moment the time is up, even if you are in the middle of a sentence.

listening.title: Earthquake early warning systems
listening.titleVi: Hệ thống cảnh báo sớm động đất
listening.context: A geophysics lecturer explains how earthquake early warning systems work and what limits them.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on earthquake early warning systems. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon, everyone. Today I want to look at a branch of geophysics with a very practical purpose: earthquake early warning. I should say at the outset that this is not earthquake prediction. Nobody can yet say that a quake will happen next Tuesday. What a warning system does is much more modest, and in some ways more useful. It tells you that a quake has just started, and that shaking is on its way.

To see how this is possible, we need to remember that an earthquake does not arrive as a single shock. When rock breaks deep underground, it sends out two main kinds of wave. The first, called the primary wave, is the faster one, and it travels through the crust at roughly six kilometres per second. It moves the ground in a push-and-pull motion, and it rarely causes much damage. The second, the secondary wave, is slower, at about three and a half kilometres per second, but it shakes the ground from side to side, and it is responsible for most of the destruction.

That difference in speed is the whole basis of early warning. The fast wave is detected by sensors close to the source, a computer estimates where the quake is and how big it is, and an alert races ahead of the slower wave at the speed of a radio signal. So how much time does that buy? At a distance of a hundred kilometres from the source, the damaging wave arrives about twelve seconds after the first one. At two hundred kilometres, the gap roughly doubles, to about twenty-four seconds.

Twelve seconds may sound trivial, but it is enough to do useful things. A person can step away from a window, a driver can stop before a tunnel, and a surgeon can pause an operation. However, there is a basic limit. In the area immediately around the source, which extends roughly thirty kilometres in every direction, the damaging wave arrives before any alert can be sent. This region is known as the blind zone, and no system can warn the people who live in it.

Now let's look at the equipment. The key instrument is the seismometer, which measures ground movement. The challenge is that the surface of the Earth is never quiet. Passing lorries, machinery, wind and even waves on the coast create vibration, and if a sensor responds to that, it will produce false alarms. For this reason, the most sensitive instruments are installed deep underground, in narrow holes drilled for the purpose, called boreholes. Some countries also lay sensors on the seabed, because many large earthquakes begin beneath the ocean, and every second of extra warning is valuable.

Several regions now run early warning systems. One country in East Asia launched a nationwide public service in two thousand and seven, after many years of development, though its railways had used a simpler version of the idea long before that. When the alert sounds, the effects can be automatic. Trains slow down and stop, lifts open at the nearest floor, gas supplies are shut off, and the doors of fire stations swing open so that the engines can leave without delay.

Others have taken different approaches. On the west coast of North America, for example, the alert is sent to mobile phones and to the screens of public buildings. The success of any of these systems depends not only on the technology but on what people do in the few seconds they have.

So much for the successes. Let me now turn to some limitations, because there are several. The first concerns accuracy in the opening seconds. When an earthquake begins, the early data from the first few sensors can look very similar for a moderate event and for a catastrophic one. A very powerful quake can therefore be mistaken, at first, for a smaller one, and the warning may underestimate the area that will be affected. Engineers deal with this by revising the estimate as more sensors report, but each revision takes time, and time is the one thing we do not have.

The second limitation is cost. A dense network of high-quality instruments is extremely expensive to install and maintain, and in many poorer regions, where earthquakes are often the most deadly, building such a network is simply out of reach. This is a cruel irony, because the buildings in those regions are frequently the least able to withstand shaking.

One promising answer is to use equipment that already exists. Nearly every modern mobile phone contains tiny motion detectors, called accelerometers, which respond when the device is shaken. A single phone is not very reliable, because it might be dropped or thrown. But if thousands of phones in the same area detect shaking at the same moment, the pattern is a strong sign of a real earthquake. Researchers are now testing systems in which millions of handsets act together as a vast, cheap network that costs the authorities almost nothing to operate.

Of course, even the best alert is useless if people do not respond sensibly. A message has to be short and clear, because there is no time to read a long explanation. The behaviour that experts recommend is simple. Get down low, take shelter under something solid, such as a strong table, and hold on to it until the shaking stops. In the English-speaking world this is usually summarised as: drop, cover and hold on.

There is one more point which I think matters a great deal. Studies of earthquakes show that, in the first seconds, people often freeze, or they run outside, which can be more dangerous than staying put, because bricks and glass fall from buildings into the street. Practice is the cure. That is why schools and workplaces in earthquake regions hold regular drills, so that the correct movements become automatic and no one has to think when the alert sounds.

There is also the question of public trust. If a system sends an alert for a quake that never reaches people, they may stop paying attention next time. Designers therefore face a difficult trade-off between speed and certainty. Wait too long, and the warning arrives too late. Send too soon, and some alerts will turn out to be wrong. Most agencies choose to accept a few false alarms rather than risk missing a real event, but they must explain this honestly to the public.

To sum up, early warning cannot stop an earthquake, and it cannot protect those closest to the source. What it can do, with only seconds to spare, is give millions of people the chance to protect themselves. Next week we will look at what happens afterwards, and how engineers decide which buildings are safe to enter.

listening.title: Registering for an evening cooking class
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký lớp nấu ăn buổi tối
listening.context: A woman phones a cooking school to register for a six-week evening course.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a woman phoning a cooking school to register for an evening course. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good evening, Quennell Kitchen School, Rowan speaking. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a place on one of your six-week evening cooking courses. A colleague at work said I could register over the phone.
Yes, that's no problem at all. I'll fill in your registration form while we talk, and then you only need to turn up on the first night. Could I have your full name, please?
It's Mirela Treharne.
Could you spell the surname for me?
Of course. T, R, E, H, A, R, N, E.
Thank you. And what's the best number to reach you on?
I have a landline at home, but nobody ever answers it, so please use my mobile. It's oh double seven double oh, nine double oh, two seven five.
Let me read that back to you. Oh double seven double oh, nine double oh, two seven five. Is that correct?
Yes, that's right.
Lovely. And may I ask how you first heard about the school?

Well, a friend of mine called Julia has done two of your courses and she is always telling me how much she enjoys them. But I actually came across your name on a leaflet in my local library last month, and that's what made me look at your website.

That's good to know, because we put leaflets in about twenty libraries across the region. Now, which course did you have in mind? We have Italian pasta, Thai cooking, bread making and a vegetarian course this term.
I was hoping for the Italian pasta course, because I'd like to make my own ravioli.
Ah, I'm afraid that one is completely full. It was the first to sell out, as it always is. There are still places on the Thai course, though, and it's very popular too.
I've never tried to cook Thai food at home, so that sounds like a good challenge. I'll go for that, please.
Excellent. The Thai course runs on Wednesday evenings and also on Saturday mornings. Which would you prefer?
I'm at my sister's every Saturday, so it will have to be Wednesday evenings.
Wednesday it is. Now, do you have any food allergies we should know about? The teachers always like to plan ahead.
I'm not vegetarian and I can eat nuts, but I'm allergic to celery. It's in a lot of sauces and stocks, so I have to be careful.
I'll make a note of that and tell the teacher before the first class. Thank you for letting us know.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Can you tell me how much the course costs?

Each class is thirty pounds, which would make a hundred and eighty for the six weeks. However, if you pay the whole fee in advance, we take a discount, so the total comes to one hundred and sixty-eight pounds. That includes all of the ingredients.
That's very reasonable. I'd rather pay in one go. And what time should I arrive?
The doors open at seven, so you have time to meet the other students and have a cup of tea, but the class itself begins at half past seven and finishes at nine thirty.
Perfect. Do I need to bring anything, such as an apron or knives?
No, the school provides aprons, knives and all the equipment. What you do need to bring is a container, because you will take home whatever you cook, and a lot of people forget.
I'll take one of my plastic tubs. I suppose I'll be eating curry all week, which is no bad thing.
Exactly. One more thing, about parking. The car park in front of the school is closed for building work this term, so please use the one behind the church, which is about two minutes away on foot.
Is there a charge for that car park?
Not after six o'clock in the evening, so you will not need any change. I'll send you a confirmation email tonight with a map attached, and you can write back if you have any questions.
How many people will be in the class? I'm a little nervous, because I'm not a very confident cook, and I'd hate to be left behind.

There are never more than twelve students, and the teacher walks round the kitchen to help everybody individually. Most of our beginners say that the first evening is the most nervous one, and by the third week they are chatting happily and sharing tips. On the last night every student receives a certificate and a small recipe booklet to keep.
That's reassuring. I'll tell my colleague, too, in case she wants to come along. Thank you very much, Rowan. I'm really looking forward to it.
You're welcome, Mirela. We'll see you on the first Wednesday.

listening.title: Changes to household recycling collections
listening.titleVi: Thay đổi lịch thu gom rác tái chế của hội đồng địa phương
listening.context: A local radio presenter reports on changes to household recycling collections in the district.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a local radio presenter talking about changes to household recycling collections. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, and welcome to the Ravenbrook local news. If you live in the district, you may have noticed a leaflet from the council on your doormat this week. It explains some big changes to the way your recycling is collected, and I've been finding out what they will mean for you.

First, the timing. The changes were originally planned for the beginning of January, but the new collection lorries arrived late, so the council has moved everything back. The new system will start on the first Monday in March. That is not next week, as some listeners have been asking me, but a little over a month from now, so there is plenty of time to get ready.

Now, why is the council doing this at all? Some residents have suggested that people asked for fewer collections, and others have said it is because of a new national law. Neither is correct. Government targets for recycling do exist, but the law does not require this particular change. The real reason is that around one load in five delivered to the sorting plant was being rejected, because it was dirty or contained the wrong kind of plastic, or had food waste mixed in. Rejected loads are sent to landfill, and that costs the council a great deal of money.

So, what will actually change? Let's start with plastic bottles, food tins and cans. The council first proposed collecting these every two weeks. However, more than four thousand residents replied to the consultation, and the great majority said that every two weeks would not be often enough, particularly for large families. The council listened, and plastic and cans will continue to be collected every week.

Paper and card, on the other hand, will move to every two weeks, because the volumes are much more predictable. And glass will no longer go into the main bin at all. Instead, every household will receive a small green box for bottles and jars, which will be emptied once every four weeks. You will not need to apply for one. They will be delivered to your door during February.

Next, the garden waste service. At the moment the brown bins are collected all year round, but the figures show that in the winter months most of them are almost empty. So from March, garden waste will be collected only between March and November, with no collections in December, January or February. People who pay for the service will get a refund for the winter months, and the council says it will be applied automatically.

What about the occasions when a collection is missed? Many people tell me that the council phone line is always busy, and the good news is that you will no longer need to use it. The phone line for missed bins is closing. Instead, you should report it on the council's website within two days of the missed collection. If you leave your bin out and do nothing, the crew will not return automatically, so do remember to report it.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Finally, a number of streets will have a different collection day, and it is important to check yours. I'll go through the areas which are changing and, for those which are not, I'll let you know.

The Brookside Estate, which has always been collected on a Monday, will move to Tuesday. Marsh Lane was previously collected on a Wednesday, but it will take over the Monday slot that Brookside is leaving. Residents in Kingsway, who are used to a Tuesday collection, will move to Thursday. The Orchards, on the other hand, will have their bins emptied on a Wednesday from March, a change from their old Friday collection.

The only area in this list that stays exactly as it is, is the Old Town, which remains on a Friday. I have also had questions about weekends. There will be no household collections on a Saturday or a Sunday under the new system. The Saturday collections in the town centre are for shops and businesses only, and they are not affected.

A few other details to finish. Bulky items such as old sofas or fridges can still be collected, at a charge of twenty-two pounds for up to three items, and you need to book that online as well. The council will also run drop-in sessions at the library on the first two Saturdays of February, where staff will be happy to answer questions and show you which items go in which container. If you would like the leaflet in a larger print size, or in another language, that is available on request.

One more practical point. The council is also introducing a free text message reminder service. You register your postcode on the website, and the evening before each collection you will receive a short message telling you which bins to put out. It is especially useful during the first few weeks, when everyone is getting used to the new timetable, and it can be switched off at any time if you find it annoying.

Residents who would find it difficult to carry their bins to the kerb, for example because of an injury or a disability, can ask for an assisted collection, so that the crew will collect the bins from beside the house. That is a free service, but it has to be arranged in advance, and the council has asked me to say that the form is available at all the libraries as well as online.
That is all the recycling news for now. After the break, we'll hear from the owner of a bakery in Old Town whose cakes have won a national prize, and then it is on to the weather.

listening.title: Presenting a study of hospital signs
listening.titleVi: Thuyết trình nghiên cứu về biển chỉ dẫn trong bệnh viện
listening.context: Two students discuss their presentation on the signs in a hospital with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Freya and Yusuf, discussing a presentation about hospital signs with their tutor, Dr Abara. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Right, let's make a start. I've looked through your draft slides on the signs at the city hospital, and I have a few thoughts. First, remind me why you picked this subject.
It comes from something that happened to Yusuf last year. His grandmother was admitted to the hospital, and he spent nearly twenty minutes just trying to find her ward.

I'm embarrassed to say it was more like half an hour. The design module gave us the method for the project, and I did read about a new hospital opening in the north of the city, but it was that walk around the corridors that made me curious about why it was so hard.
A real experience of being lost is a very good motivation. Now, tell me about the observation itself.
We stood near the main entrance and watched forty visitors, noting where they hesitated, who they asked for directions, and how long it took them to get to the right lift.
Forty people is quite enough for a short study like this, so don't apologise for that. What worries me is when you watched them. You tell me you only went on two weekday mornings.
That's true. We both have lectures in the afternoons.

The trouble is that on weekday mornings the entrance is full of staff and patients who come every week, and they already know the building. The people who struggle most are first-time visitors, and many of them come at weekends. So your picture of the problem may be too mild, and you need to say that openly.
We could go back on a Saturday before we present. It would only take a morning. We could also note how busy the lifts were, and whether it was dry, since neither of those came up in our notes.

That would certainly help. I'd also like you to think about the weather on the days you watched, because rain can change how visitors behave, for instance by making them hurry inside without looking around at all. Now, I'd like to hear your own views. Yusuf, you wrote in your notes that you prefer the coloured lines on the floor to any other kind of sign. Why is that?

Because they are so straightforward. You follow the blue line and you arrive at the X-ray department, and there is nothing to read or to remember. Out of everything we looked at, I think that is the clearest way of guiding people, and I'd like to see more of it.
I'm a little less enthusiastic. Some people can't tell certain colours apart, and a line on the floor is no use at all when the corridor is crowded.
Both of those points belong in your presentation. Now, you also recommend removing the written words from every sign and replacing them with symbols. I have doubts about that.
We thought symbols would help people who do not speak English well.

In some cases they would, but a symbol is only useful if everybody reads it the same way, and that isn't always true. Older visitors in particular often find a plain word easier than a picture. As it stands, your recommendation overlooks people who depend on the written words, so I'd suggest keeping the text and adding the symbols next to it.
That's a fair point. We'll change it.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Let's look at what the visitors told you. You asked each person what had made the journey hard. What came up most often?
The text was far too small. Nearly everyone mentioned that. A lot of the writing is the same size as the notices about hand washing, so it disappears completely against the walls.
The other big one was the names of the departments. Words like cardiology or orthopaedics mean nothing to most people. They would much rather see heart clinic or bones and joints.
Did anyone say the signs were hung too high?
Only two or three people. The lighting was criticised even less, and just one person thought that an arrow was pointing the wrong way.
So those first two findings are the heart of your report. Make sure they get a slide each.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Now, some advice on each part of the presentation. Yusuf, you open with a long description of how the hospital is organised, and there is not a single image. Your audience has never seen those corridors, so show them some photographs of the signs that confused people. That will draw them in straight away.
I have plenty of pictures on my phone. I'll choose the three worst.
Next, the method. You say you stood at the main entrance. Please explain why you chose that spot in particular, rather than the emergency entrance or the car park. Someone is bound to ask.
Because it is the busiest door and the one that most first-time visitors use. I'll put that on the slide.

Good. Then the results. You have twelve slides of charts at the moment, and the audience will be exhausted long before the end. Cut them down to about half and keep only the ones that support your main points.
I was afraid you'd say that. I'm quite attached to a couple of them.

I know, but the others can go in your handout. Finally, the conclusion. You finish by repeating your findings, which is fine, but you also have the chance to say what a hospital could do next, for example testing a new sign in a single department for a month. A practical idea is what examiners remember.
That's a good idea. We could suggest a trial in the outpatient clinic.

One more practical suggestion. Bring a printed copy of your slides on the day, in case the projector fails or the file refuses to open. It happens more often than you would imagine, and a calm, well-prepared pair of presenters can recover very quickly.
We'll print two copies, one each, and keep a spare on a memory stick.

You don't need to worry about timing. You were at eleven minutes in your practice run, which leaves you a comfortable margin, and you already give plenty of figures, so there is no need to add any more.
Great. We'll send you the new slides on Friday.
I look forward to them. Good luck with the Saturday visit.

options: a news report about a new hospital

listening.title: The economics of ancient trade routes
listening.titleVi: Kinh tế học của các tuyến thương mại cổ đại
listening.context: A lecturer in economic history explains how costs, risk and institutions shaped trade in the ancient world.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on the economics of ancient trade routes. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Today I want to look at ancient trade routes through the eyes of an economist rather than a traveller. Historians have written wonderful accounts of caravans and merchant ships, but I'd like to ask a different question. Why did goods move along certain routes and not others? I'll approach this by looking at three things: the cost of transport, the problem of risk, and the way trading communities organised themselves.

Let's begin with the cost of transport, because it determined which goods could be traded at all. In the overland trade, the most important animal was the camel. A typical camel could carry a load of about two hundred and fifty kilograms, which is considerably more than a horse or a donkey. Even so, it covered only thirty to forty kilometres a day, and every animal needed feeding and watering, with the cost of the guides and guards on top. The result was that a journey of several months multiplied the cost of the goods many times over.

This had an important consequence. Nobody was going to send a heavy cargo of grain or timber across a continent, because the transport would cost more than the goods were worth. Long-distance traders concentrated instead on goods that were light but of great value, such as silk, spices, incense and precious stones. A single bag of the right spice could pay for the whole journey, and that is why these luxury goods dominate our picture of ancient trade, even though the vast majority of what people actually ate and used was produced locally.

Now compare that with the sea. Moving goods by water was always far cheaper. Historians have tried to estimate the difference, and one careful study suggests that sea freight cost roughly twenty per cent of what the same cargo would have cost to move overland. That explains why the great cities of the ancient world almost all stood on coasts or on navigable rivers, and why bulky goods such as grain could be shipped across the Mediterranean in large quantities.

The sea had its own difficulties, of course, and the sailors of the Indian Ocean solved one of them very cleverly. They discovered that the winds in that region do not blow in a single direction all year round. Instead, they reverse with the seasons, a pattern we call the monsoon. Mariners learned to time their voyages accordingly, sailing east with the summer winds and returning with the opposite winds in winter. Once that knowledge was widely shared, a round trip between Arabia and India that had once taken years could be completed in a single season.

That brings me to the second theme, risk. Every long journey was dangerous, and I do not only mean storms and bandits. Along land routes the cost that worried merchants most was a human one. Each time a caravan crossed the territory of a new ruler, it had to pay. Rulers could not collect taxes from people who were only passing through, so they placed tolls at every border, at bridges and at wells. Some of these charges were modest, but they accumulated, and a merchant who failed to budget for them could arrive at his destination with no profit at all.

At sea the principal danger was shipwreck, and here merchants developed a strategy that economists today would recognise instantly. They never put their whole fortune in one place. A careful trader would spread a consignment across a number of different vessels, so that the loss of any single one would be painful but not ruinous. In effect, this was a primitive form of insurance, and the more developed ports even had specialist lenders who charged very high interest on loans that were repaid only if the ship arrived safely.

The third theme is institutions, and it is where trade routes become truly interesting. Think about what trading across a thousand kilometres actually required. You had to trust a partner whom you might never meet again, in a place where your own government had no authority, and without any court that could force him to keep his word. How did people manage? One answer was that certain cities grew rich simply because they stood where several routes met. Such cities became trading hubs. Merchants from many regions could store their goods safely and exchange them for goods from somewhere else, so that nobody had to make the entire journey from one end of the route to the other.

The second answer was reputation. In a world without enforceable contracts, a merchant's good name was the most valuable thing he owned. Those who cheated would find that no one would deal with them again, and word travelled fast along the routes. Some trading communities went further and policed themselves. They kept records of who had failed to pay, and they excluded those people from the market.

The third answer is an early financial invention. Carrying large amounts of coin across dangerous country was an invitation to robbery, so merchants began to use written promises of payment. A trader would hand over a sum in one city and receive a document that his partner in another city would honour. This was an early system of credit, and it freed merchants from carrying heavy coin. It also shows us something about the ancient economy that is easy to miss. Some of its most sophisticated tools had been developed by people who were not rulers or philosophers, but ordinary traders solving practical problems.

Finally, let me touch on what travelled besides goods. Silk and spices left the most visible traces in the archaeological record, but historians increasingly argue that the most lasting cargo was knowledge. Numbers, farming techniques, religious beliefs and stories moved along the same roads as the merchandise, and in the long run they transformed the societies that received them far more profoundly than any luxury ever did. So when we study ancient trade routes, we should keep in mind that the exchange of ideas may in the end have mattered more than the exchange of goods.

I should add a warning here. Our evidence for all of this is uneven. Coins, wrecks and the occasional clay tablet survive, but the everyday lives of small traders are mostly invisible to us, and every estimate I have given today carries a margin of error that I would not like you to forget.

To sum up, then, transport costs decided what was traded, risk decided how it was organised, and trust made the whole system possible. In next week's seminar, we'll look at how these ideas apply to the first great trading empires, and I'd like you to read the two short chapters on the reading list beforehand.

listening.title: Volunteering at an animal rescue centre
listening.titleVi: Đăng ký làm tình nguyện viên ở trại cứu hộ động vật
listening.context: A man phones an animal rescue centre to sign up as a weekend volunteer.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning an animal rescue centre to sign up as a volunteer. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Hollowbrook Animal Rescue, Megan speaking.
Hello. I saw your notice in the library asking for new volunteers, and I wondered whether I could sign up over the phone.
You can, and thank you for getting in touch. We are always short of helpers, especially at weekends. I'll fill in the volunteer form while we talk. Can I have your surname first, please?
It's Gavin Pemberton. P, E, M, B, E, R, T, O, N.
Thanks, Gavin. And a mobile number, in case we need to change a shift at short notice?
Sure. It's zero double seven double zero, six one four, three eight two.
Got it. Now, which part of the centre would you like to work in? We have the dog kennels, the cat room, and the small animal unit, which looks after the rabbits and guinea pigs.
I've always had dogs, so I assumed I would ask for the kennels. I'm a bit worried, though, because I know the dog walkers have to be here on weekday mornings, and I work then.

Yes, that is a problem. The dog team do their walks between nine and twelve on weekdays. The cat room, on the other hand, needs extra pairs of hands at the weekend, mainly for cleaning and feeding, and for talking to visitors who are thinking of adopting.
Then the cats it is. I don't know much about them, but I'm willing to learn.
That's fine, because we give every new person full training. Have you worked with animals before?
Not professionally. But I spent two summers at a boarding kennel near my parents' house, helping to clean the runs and feed the dogs. I also had a rabbit when I was a child, if that counts.
Both count, but the kennel experience is especially useful, so I'll put that on the form. Now, which day would suit you?
I'd prefer Sunday, if possible, because I play football on Saturday mornings.
I'm afraid our Sunday team is already complete. But the cat room stays open to visitors until four on Saturdays, so you could come in the afternoon.
In that case Saturday is fine. I can play football in the morning and come to you after lunch.

Lovely. All new volunteers must attend an induction session before they start. There are two coming up. The first is on the seventh of March, but that one is fully booked, so the next one is on the fourteenth.
The fourteenth is fine. Do I need to bring anything with me?

Just yourself, and a pair of sensible shoes. The induction takes about two hours, and you will meet the other people in the cat team. After that you can start your first real shift the following weekend.
That sounds good. I'm quite looking forward to it already. My flatmate keeps telling me I should do something useful with my free time.
Well, you will certainly be useful here. Some of our cats have been waiting for a home for months, and they really do enjoy having a regular person who sits and talks to them.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Do I have to pay for anything? I don't mind, but I'd like to know in advance.

Nothing for the training. We give every volunteer a green fleece jacket to wear on site, and there is a ten-pound deposit, which you get back if you return the fleece when you stop volunteering. The T-shirt is free.
Fair enough. How long is a typical shift?

Most of our volunteers do three hours. The dog walkers can do two hours, because walks are tiring, but in the cat room we ask for a minimum of three, so that the animals see the same face for a decent time.
That's no problem. Is there anything I need to do for my health?

Yes. We ask all volunteers to have an up-to-date tetanus injection, because of the risk of scratches and bites. If you haven't had one in the last ten years, your doctor can arrange it, and it's free.
I think I had one for my travels, but I'll check. And where do I park? I'll be coming by car.
We're about a mile outside the village, and there is a gravel car park behind the old barn. Please don't leave your car in the lane, because it blocks the vet's van when there is an emergency.
Understood. I'll make sure I use the car park.
Good. I'll email you a confirmation by Friday, with a map and the exact time of the induction. If anything changes, ring this number and ask for me. Thanks again for offering to help, Gavin.
Thank you, Megan. See you on the fourteenth.
