listening.title: Introducing a maritime museum
listening.titleVi: Hướng dẫn viên giới thiệu bảo tàng hàng hải
listening.context: A guide welcomes visitors to a museum of sailing and trade and explains what they can see.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a guide welcoming a group of visitors to a maritime museum. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good morning, everyone, and welcome to the Saltmarsh Maritime Museum. My name is Elena, and I'll be your guide for the next hour. Before we go inside, let me tell you a little about the building and about how the museum works.

Many visitors guess that this was once a shipyard office, because of the anchors by the door, and some think it was a hospital for sailors. In fact it was built as a customs warehouse, and it stored tea, spices and timber before they were taxed. The thick walls and the heavy iron doors date from that time.

The museum has been here for thirty years, and it has four main galleries, a boat shed in the courtyard and a small café. We are open from ten to five every day. On Thursdays, however, we stay open until eight in the evening, and that is the best time to come if you prefer a quiet visit. The café stops serving at seven, so you can have a meal before you leave.

A word about photography. Many people think they cannot take pictures in museums, but here you are welcome to photograph almost everything. Please switch off your flash, though, because the light slowly damages old paper and paint. And please do not touch the objects, however tempting. Several of them are more than two hundred years old.

Some of you have asked about our restoration work. The biggest project of recent years was the museum's lifeboat, which was found rotting in a field and took three years to repair. It was finished only last spring, and it now has a building of its own, so you will not find it in the main galleries. The schooner model took even longer, but that was cleaned and repainted some time ago.

If you have brought children, they will enjoy our explorer trail. Ask at the desk for a free trail sheet, and as they walk round the galleries they can collect a stamp at each of five stations. Anyone who finds all five gets a small badge from the shop. We also have costumes and a craft workshop, but those run only in the school holidays and need to be booked in advance, and there is a small charge for them.
Now, are there any questions about the practical side? No? Then let's go through the galleries one by one, and I'll tell you where to find the things people most often ask about.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: We start here, in the entrance hall. The first thing you see is our wooden figurehead, the carved woman at the front of a ship, which was taken from a trading vessel that sank in the harbour long ago. She is nearly three metres tall, and visitors often ask whether she is a real person. She is not. The carver said she was the spirit of the wind.

Next, take the stairs up to the mezzanine. The big model of a trading schooner used to stand in the entrance hall, where you could walk all round it, but we moved it up to the mezzanine last year because the hall was becoming crowded. It now sits under a glass case with its own lighting, and it is more detailed than you might expect, with tiny ropes and even small barrels on the deck.

On the floor below the mezzanine is the lower deck. This is a full-size copy of the sailors' sleeping quarters, and it is where the children's trail begins. It is dark and quite cramped, but it is good fun. The room next to it, the harbour room, is where we serve coffee and where most visitors take a break halfway round.

The rope loft is the long room at the top of the building. We first thought of showing the sailors' letters on the lower deck, but there was not enough light for people to read them. In the rope loft you can sit and read the handwriting at your own speed. Some of the letters are very moving, written by young sailors who had not seen their families for two years.

Beyond the rope loft is the navigation room. Here you will find our collection of brass sextants and chronometers, which sailors used to find their position at sea. If you are interested in how a ship crossed an ocean without any satellites, I would suggest staying here a little longer than in the other rooms.

Finally, the lifeboat. As I said, it has its own building, the boat shed, across the courtyard. You reach it through the door beside the café. It is very big, and you can climb the steps and look inside it, but please keep your hands off the oars.

We also have a small shop by the exit. It sells postcards, books about the sea, and some beautiful old maps that are printed from our own archive. Everything sold in the shop helps to pay for the conservation work, so please do spend some money there.

One last practical point. Audio guides are available at the desk in English, French and German, and they are included in the ticket price. If you would rather sit down for a while, there are benches in every gallery, and the staff can lend a folding stool to anyone who finds standing difficult. Lockers for large bags are free and are in the corridor beside the entrance hall.

Before you leave the entrance hall, please check the notice board beside the desk. It lists the talks and demonstrations that take place each day, such as knot-tying for beginners and a short film about the harbour in the last century. Most of them are free, and they usually start at eleven and at two.
We hope you enjoy your visit, and if you have any problem during the morning, just ask one of the staff in the blue jackets. Enjoy the museum.

listening.title: Planning a survey on student drinking habits
listening.titleVi: Lập kế hoạch khảo sát thói quen uống nước của sinh viên
listening.context: Two students discuss the design of a questionnaire survey on drinking water with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two students, Imogen and Dmitri, discussing a survey project with their tutor, Dr Achterberg. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Right, take a seat. Your proposal for the student drinking-habits survey arrived this morning, and I would like to go through it with you. First, tell me what you are trying to find out.

We want to know how much water students actually drink during a normal day, and whether they believe it affects their concentration. There is plenty of advice online, but very little real data about our own campus.
We also want to compare first-year students with older ones, because our guess is that people living in halls of residence have quite different routines.
Interesting. I see that you chose a questionnaire. Did you think about interviews at any point?
At first, yes, because interviews give you much richer answers. But each one would take about half an hour, and we only have six weeks in total.
With a questionnaire we can reach several hundred students instead of twenty, so that is why we decided to go that way.
A reasonable decision. Now let's look at the questions themselves. On the first page you ask people whether they drink a lot, a moderate amount or a little water each day.
Yes, we thought that would be quick for people to answer.

I'm afraid that is much too vague to be useful. One person's idea of a lot is another person's idea of a little. Ask for the number of glasses or bottles instead, and then you can work out an average.
That's a good point. We will change it.
You are planning to put the form online. Does anything about that worry you?
My worry is that people won't be honest. Someone who drinks hardly any water might not want to admit it, and others may exaggerate to look healthy.
That is a genuine problem with all self-reported data, although keeping the form anonymous will help. Say clearly at the top that no names are collected.
We were also thinking of a prize draw for everyone who completes it, perhaps a metal water bottle.

I like that. It is a cheap way of increasing the number of replies, and I would not worry that it spoils the results. Just make sure the draw entry is on a separate page, so that it cannot be linked to anyone's answers.
Good idea. We can do that with a second form.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, what exactly will the questionnaire cover? You have a long list of ideas on the second page.
The amount of water people drink on a typical day, obviously. We also want to ask whether they carry a refillable bottle, because the university is trying to reduce plastic waste.
I wanted to add a section on which drinks people buy at the campus café, and Imogen thought we might ask about the hours they spend studying.

I would drop both. The café question belongs in a different study, and study hours would turn your survey into something else entirely. Keep it short, because people abandon a questionnaire that takes more than ten minutes.
We could include their favourite brand of bottled water, though. A company might be interested in that.
No. Nobody is paying for this research, and the brand has nothing to do with your question. Concentrate on the amount and the bottle.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Could you also help us plan the next few weeks? We are not sure what order to do things in.
Of course. Let me go through the stages. First, the pilot. Before you send anything out, ask ten friends to fill in the questionnaire and tell you which questions confused them.
Would it be better to use strangers for that?
Friends are fine at this stage, because you only want to catch mistakes in the wording. Now, how will you distribute it? You mentioned posters with a code to scan.
Yes, that was our idea. We would put them up in the library and the main corridors.
Posters bring in very few replies, I'm afraid. Ask the student union to email the link to all members. That reaches far more people, and they are more likely to open a message from the union.
How long should we keep the survey open? We thought one day would be enough.
A day is far too short. Leave it open for two weeks, and send one reminder after the first week. More than one reminder irritates people, and then they stop reading your emails altogether.
Should we ask lecturers to mention the survey in their classes?
That would be nice, but it is not essential, so do not spend time chasing people for it.
And what about the final presentation? We have so many numbers from the first-year and older groups that I'm not sure how to show them.
Keep it to a few key charts. A table with fifty numbers will lose the audience, and each chart should carry one clear message. You will have only ten minutes, so choose carefully.
One thing we have not discussed is ethics. Do we need permission from anyone before we start?

Yes. Even a simple survey needs approval from the department's ethics committee, and you must submit the form at least ten days before you begin. Include a short information sheet that explains what the survey is for, how long it takes and what will happen to the answers. It should also say that taking part is voluntary, and that anyone can stop at any point without giving a reason.
What if some students are under eighteen? A few first-year students might be.

Good question. For a survey of this kind it is normally acceptable, because nothing in it is sensitive, but the committee will tell you for certain. Do not guess about this, and do not start collecting any data until you have a written reply. It is the one deadline that you cannot move, and I have seen projects lose a whole month because the form was sent late.

Then we will submit it this week. We would like to have the pilot finished before the end of the month, and we would also like to leave enough time to write the report calmly, rather than the night before the deadline.
A sensible attitude. Work backwards from the hand-in date and write down a date for every stage, then put the list where you can both see it.
That is really helpful. Thank you, Dr Achterberg. We will send you the revised questionnaire by Friday.
You are welcome. Remember to keep a copy of all your data in two places, in case something goes wrong with a computer. Good luck with the pilot, both of you.

listening.title: Storing renewable energy
listening.titleVi: Các kỹ thuật lưu trữ năng lượng tái tạo
listening.context: A lecturer in energy engineering compares the main ways of storing electricity from wind and solar power.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture about storing renewable energy. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good afternoon. Today I want to talk about a problem that sounds simple but is not: what do we do with renewable electricity when nobody needs it, and how do we get it back when everybody does? The sun does not shine at night, and the wind drops without warning, so storage is the key to a grid that runs mostly on renewables.

Let me begin with the oldest technology, pumped hydro. The idea has been around for about a hundred years. When there is more electricity than the grid needs, the surplus is used to drive pumps, and water is pumped uphill into a reservoir. Later, when demand rises, the water is released and runs back down through turbines, generating power again.

Pumped hydro is by far the biggest form of storage in the world today. It is reliable and it can last for decades. Its weakness is geography. You need two reservoirs at different heights, close together, which means suitable terrain, and that rules out flat countries and most densely populated regions. Building such a plant also takes many years and plenty of money.

The second technology is the one you all know, the battery. Lithium-ion batteries have moved from phones to cars to grids, and the reason is simple: the cost has fallen by roughly ninety per cent in little more than a decade. This is partly because of mass production for electric vehicles, which has turned out to be a gift for the energy industry.

But lithium-ion batteries have a limit. They lose capacity slowly as they are charged and discharged, which engineers call degradation. After perhaps ten or fifteen years a grid battery has to be replaced, and that replacement cost must be included when you compare technologies. There are also concerns about the mining of lithium and cobalt, which I will come back to at the end.

Now, a less familiar alternative: the flow battery. In a conventional battery, the chemicals that store the energy are packed in the same box as the electrodes. In a flow battery they are kept apart. The energy is stored in two liquids, which are held in two large tanks and pumped through a cell when electricity is needed.

The advantage is flexibility. If you want to store more energy, you do not build a new battery, you simply fit bigger tanks. Flow batteries can also be charged and emptied thousands of times with very little damage, so they last much longer than lithium-ion cells. On the other hand, they are bulky and more complicated, which means they suit large fixed sites and not vehicles.

Next, a technology that sounds strange the first time you hear it: compressed air. When power is cheap, electric compressors squeeze air at high pressure into underground spaces, usually old salt caverns, where it can be held for a long time. When the grid needs electricity, the air is let out, heated and passed through a turbine.

The difficulty is that compressing air produces heat, and in the simplest plants that heat is simply lost. Newer designs capture it and store it in a tank of hot stones or water, and then use it again when the air expands. That makes the process much more efficient, but it adds to the cost, and you still need the right kind of underground rock.

Let me mention one more mechanical idea, because it comes up in student projects every year: gravity storage. A crane or a lift raises heavy concrete blocks when there is spare power, and lowers them to generate electricity later. It is neat, and it uses no unusual materials, but the amount of energy stored is rather small unless the blocks are enormous, so for now it is more of an interesting experiment than a serious competitor.

The last technology on my list is hydrogen, and it is the one that excites the most people. The principle is that surplus power is used for electrolysis, which splits water into hydrogen and oxygen. The hydrogen can then be stored in tanks or underground, and later burned or fed to a fuel cell to make electricity again.

What makes hydrogen special is time. A battery that sits full for weeks will leak a little energy, and a pumped hydro reservoir loses water to evaporation. Hydrogen, in contrast, can be stored for months with almost no loss, which means that summer sunshine could in principle heat a house in winter. No other technology offers this ability to move energy between seasons.

The drawback is efficiency. At each step, from electricity to hydrogen and back to electricity, energy is lost. Depending on the equipment, only about a third of the original power comes back out. A lithium-ion battery returns around nine-tenths. So hydrogen only makes sense for long periods of storage, where its other advantages outweigh the waste, and for jobs that are hard to electrify, such as steel production or shipping.

So which of these will win? I would like to be able to give you one answer, but I cannot. Most experts now expect that no single technology will be enough. Short-term balancing, from minutes up to a few hours, is best done by batteries. Daily cycles suit pumped hydro, flow batteries or compressed air, depending on the local landscape. And for the long gaps, hydrogen is the most promising candidate. The grid of the future will therefore rely on a combination of several technologies, each doing the job it is best at.

I should also say something about the economics. Storage is paid for in several ways. Some owners earn money by buying electricity when it is cheap and selling it when it is dear, which is called arbitrage. Others are paid by the grid operator simply for being ready to respond within seconds if something fails. Regulation matters a great deal, because in some countries a storage plant is charged twice, once as a consumer and once as a generator, and that can ruin the business case. Engineers sometimes forget that policy decisions can be as important as chemistry.

Let me end with the environmental side. Every technology I have described has a footprint. Pumped hydro changes valleys and rivers, batteries need mined metals, and hydrogen needs a great deal of clean electricity to start with. For that reason, one of the most active areas of research is recycling, so that the metals in old batteries can be recovered and used again. A recycled cell can contain materials that are worth more than the cell itself.

For next week, please read the two short papers on the course page and think about the following question: for an island with strong winds but no mountains, which combination of technologies would you choose, and why? Thank you.

listening.title: Booking a holiday cottage
listening.titleVi: Đặt nhà nghỉ cho kỳ nghỉ gia đình
listening.context: A man phones a holiday cottage agency to book a cottage for a family holiday by the sea.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a holiday cottage agency to book a cottage for a family holiday. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good afternoon, Coastline Cottages, Gwen speaking. How can I help you?
Hello. I'd like to book a cottage for a family holiday this summer. I saw your brochure at a friend's house, and I've been looking at your website as well.
Lovely. I'll take your details first, and then we can look at availability. Could I have your surname, please?
It's Ravenscroft.
Could you spell that for me?
Of course. R, A, V, E, N, S, C, R, O, F, T.
Thank you, Mr Ravenscroft. And a contact number, in case we need to reach you about the booking?
The best number is oh one six three two, nine six oh, seven two five.
Got it. Now, which of our cottages were you interested in? Do you have one in mind?
Yes, I liked the look of Primrose Cottage. It's the one with the little garden and the view over the harbour.

Ah, I'm afraid Primrose is fully booked all through August. It's very popular with families. But we do have Larkspur Cottage, which is just along the lane. It has the same view, and the kitchen is a little bigger.
Does it have a garden?
A small terrace rather than a garden, but there is a table and chairs, and the view of the harbour is just as good.
That sounds fine. We'll take Larkspur, then.
Wonderful. What dates were you thinking of?
We wanted to arrive on the tenth of August.
Let me check. Ah, there's a problem there. Larkspur is occupied until the sixteenth, so the earliest you could arrive is the seventeenth.
That's all right. The seventeenth works for us, because the children don't go back to school until September anyway.
Then I'll put you down for the seventeenth of August. How many people will be staying?
There will be four of us, my wife, our two children and me. Actually, hold on. My parents have just asked whether they can join us, so that makes six.
Larkspur sleeps up to six, so that's no problem at all. Do you need anything extra, such as a cot or a highchair?
Our little girl is eighteen months old. We have our own travel cot, but a highchair would be very useful.
I'll arrange that for you, and there's no charge. Is there anything else you'd like to ask before we go on?
I don't think so. Please carry on.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Could you tell me how much the cottage will cost for the week?
In July and the first week of August, the weekly rent is six hundred and ninety-five pounds. From the tenth of August onwards it drops to six hundred and forty-five, so that's the rate you will pay.
That's better than I expected. And is there a deposit to pay?

Yes, there is. It's usually one hundred and fifty pounds, and we return it within a week of your departure, provided there is no damage. It rises to two hundred and fifty if you bring a pet, but you aren't planning to, are you?
No, no pets, thankfully. We have enough to look after already.
Then one hundred and fifty it is. The balance of the rent must be paid six weeks before you arrive, and I will send you a reminder by email.
Thank you. How do we get the keys? Do we need to come to your office?

No, our office is about forty miles from the coast, so that wouldn't be sensible. You collect the keys from the post office in the village. It's next to the harbour and it opens at nine. If you arrive after five, ring me and I will arrange for the keys to be left in a box beside the front door.
That's very helpful. And is the beach close? The children will want to swim every day.

The nearest beach is only five minutes away by car, but if you would rather walk, it's fifteen minutes along the cliff path. The path is fairly flat, but a little uneven in places, so you may prefer a sturdy buggy for your daughter.
We have one of those. And what about bed linen and towels?

Bed linen is included. Towels are not, so please bring your own, and bring some for the beach as well. There's a small shop in the village for anything you forget, and a larger supermarket six miles inland.
Excellent. Is there anything else we should know before we arrive?

Just one thing. The lane to the cottage is very narrow, and parking is limited to two cars, so if your parents are coming in a separate vehicle, they will need to leave it in the village car park and walk up.
Understood. They are travelling with us anyway, so it won't be a problem. Thank you for your help, Gwen.
You're very welcome, Mr Ravenscroft. I'll send the confirmation to you this afternoon, and I hope you all have a lovely holiday.

listening.title: A school open day for parents
listening.titleVi: Hiệu trưởng giới thiệu ngày mở cửa của trường cho phụ huynh
listening.context: The headteacher of a secondary school talks to parents about the arrangements for the school’s open day.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear the headteacher of a secondary school talking to parents about the school’s open day. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming. I'm Martin Dalton, the headteacher here at Elmbrook Community School. I'd like to use the next few minutes to explain what will happen on our open day, which takes place the Saturday after next, and to answer some of the questions that many of you have already sent to the office.

First, why Saturday? Some of you have asked whether we are doing it so that pupils can help with the displays. They will, and they enjoy it, but that's not the reason. In last year's survey, the biggest complaint from parents was that they simply couldn't take time off work during the week to look around. So a Saturday it is, and I hope that means many more of you will be able to come.

The doors open at ten o'clock and close at three. The most popular part of the day is the guided tour, and I'd encourage everyone to join one. Tours used to last forty-five minutes, but several parents told us that wasn't long enough to see the science block and the sports facilities properly, so this year each tour will take a full hour. They leave from the main entrance every half hour, and our older pupils will be the guides, so you can ask them anything you like.

Now, what has changed since last year? You may have heard that we refurbished the library, but that was done two years ago, so it's not new. Nor have we managed to enlarge the car park, I'm afraid. We simply don't have the land. Visitors are asked to park at the leisure centre on Mill Road, and a free minibus will bring you to the gate every ten minutes. The genuinely new feature is our indoor climbing wall, which was finished in the summer holidays. Pupils from the climbing club will be giving short demonstrations all morning, and you're welcome to watch.

A number of you have asked about admissions. If you are thinking of applying for a place next September, there will be a special talk in the lower hall at eleven o'clock and again at two. The deputy head will explain how places are offered and answer your questions. Seats are limited, so we are asking people to register in advance. Please don't telephone the office, because the lines are busy enough already. You'll find a short form on the school website, and it takes about two minutes to fill in. If you simply turn up on the day, we will do our best to find you a seat, but we can't promise.

Finally, lunch. Our catering students are preparing a buffet in the dining room between twelve and two. A ticket for an adult costs five pounds, which includes a drink. Children under twelve eat free, and the first cup of coffee is on the school. All of the money goes towards a trip for our catering students next spring, so it really is for a good cause.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now let me tell you where you can find the main events. There is a printed map in your welcome pack, but I'll go through them in the order of the programme so that you can mark them on the map as we go.

The day begins at half past ten with a concert by the school orchestra. That will be in the main hall, and it lasts about thirty-five minutes. We have almost eighty pupils in the orchestra this year, so the stage will be very full, and I'd recommend arriving a few minutes early if you want a good seat.

At eleven fifteen, our design and technology department will be showing off the robots that pupils have built this term. You will find them in the design studio, which is on the first floor of the new building. Please be careful on the stairs, because they are steep, and a lift is available at the back for anyone who needs it.

If you would like to know what it's like to learn another language here, we are running short taster sessions in Room Twelve. We teach French and Spanish, and from September we will also offer Mandarin. A pupil in each class will show you what a typical lesson looks like, and you are welcome to join in.

At lunchtime, our chemistry teachers will do some experiments in the science block. These are always very popular, so don't be surprised if there is a queue. Some of the reactions are quite loud, so if you're bringing very young children, you may wish to keep them at a distance.

Finally, there will be a sports demonstration in the afternoon. Normally you would expect that to happen in the gymnasium, and it's what the programme in your pack says. However, the floor is being repainted that week, so it will take place in the courtyard instead, weather permitting. I'm afraid the programme was printed before we knew about the painting, so please ignore what it says.

There will also be a book sale in the library all day, and the school shop will be open for anyone who needs to buy uniform. Neither of these is part of the main programme, but they are worth a visit.

Before I finish, a word about safety. Everyone must sign in at the main entrance and wear a visitor's badge. Children are welcome, but they must stay with an adult at all times. If you need to speak to a member of staff, look for someone wearing a green lanyard. Thank you again for coming, and I look forward to seeing you on the day.

listening.title: Designing a library extension
listening.titleVi: Thiết kế phần mở rộng của một thư viện
listening.context: Two architecture students discuss the design of a library extension with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two architecture students, Tamsin and Ewan, discussing the design of a library extension with their tutor, Ms Calloway. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Right, let's look at your concept design for the library extension. Tamsin, why don't you begin with the roof? Last week you were very excited about a glass roof over the main reading hall.

I was. I drew a full glass roof, because I wanted readers to feel they were sitting outdoors. But then I ran a sun-path study, and the south side would turn into a greenhouse by July. The books would suffer, and we would need so many blinds that it would defeat the whole idea.
That's a sensible conclusion. Cost is a different matter, and not one to worry about at concept stage. Heat is a real design problem, so I'm glad you tested it.
Meanwhile, I've been thinking about how the extension should sit next to the old Victorian building. The council would probably be happy if we copied the brickwork and the arched windows.
And what do you think about that approach, Ewan?
Honestly, I don't like it. Imitating old buildings always looks a little apologetic to me. I'd rather the extension was honestly modern, and let the old brick stand out beside it.
That's a legitimate position, and many well-known architects would agree with you. Tamsin, are you happy with it?
Yes, as long as the two parts are connected properly, so that people feel it is one library and not two.

Good. Now, the entrance. I looked at your plans carefully, and I have a serious concern. You have put wheelchair users on a long side ramp, while everyone else goes up the steps to the front doors. That says some visitors matter less than others, and I don't think a public library should say that.
We hadn't thought of it that way. We were only trying to fit the ramp around the old stonework.
We could drop the steps altogether and slope the whole forecourt, then use one pair of sliding doors for everyone.

That's much better. Keep that idea. Now, your presentation to the review panel. You have a lot of material and only fifteen minutes. Panels remember one clear idea better than ten. Choose your main idea and show everything else as support.
I must admit I'm a bit nervous about the presentation. Panels always seem to ask difficult questions.
They do, but a clear central idea makes the questions much easier to answer. Whenever you are asked something awkward, bring the answer back to that idea.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: Now, I want to talk about the features in your plan. You have proposed quite a long list. A garden on the roof, a café, a quiet reading gallery, a children's story room, and a display area for local history. You have space and budget for only two of those, so which will you keep?
I'd keep the roof garden. It would look wonderful in the drawings.
It would, but gardens at that height need irrigation and constant maintenance, and the wind up there is strong. A library service with a shrinking budget will not thank you for it.
Fair enough. And the café? That's what most of the students asked for in our survey.
The council already has one across the road, and a second café would simply compete with it. Drop that too.
So we keep the gallery for quiet study, and the story room.

Exactly. The first answers a need that students keep mentioning, and the second brings families in. The local history display can go in the foyer later, when the budget allows, because at the moment there is no money for display cases.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Now, materials. I'd like you to tell me what each part of the extension will be made of, and why.
For the floors, we're proposing polished concrete, laid over underfloor heating. It's hard-wearing, and the book trolleys will run easily on it.
Good choice. What about the outer walls? You were arguing about this last week.
We compromised. The walls will be reclaimed brick, taken from an old mill that is being demolished near the river. That ties the extension to the old building, but the shape stays modern.
We did think about glass bricks for part of the wall, but they are far too heavy, and they would have taken the budget over the limit. We shall use ordinary windows instead.
And the roof, now that the glass roof has gone?

Copper panels. They look warm at first, and over the years they slowly turn green, which suits the old building. Ewan wanted steel mesh for the staircase balustrade, but I'd rather save that for later.
I'd still like the steps themselves to be something special. We found a supplier of recycled timber, taken from old railway sleepers, and the treads would have a lovely colour.
I like that very much. It tells a story, and it's sustainable. Did you consider cork for the ceiling in the children's room? It would help to absorb the noise.
We did, but it's only for the acoustic lining, so it's a detail rather than one of the main materials.

Fair enough. Have you thought about how the building will be lit in the evenings? A library that glows at night can make a street feel safer, but too much light can also annoy the neighbours in the flats opposite.
We hadn't gone into that much detail yet. I suppose we could use warm, low lights in the reading gallery, and keep the main entrance brighter, so that people can see the doors from the street.
And we could put the lights on sensors in the quiet areas, so that they switch off when nobody is there. That would also reduce the running costs.

Good. Mention that in your report, because panels like to see that students have thought about the long-term use of a building and not only about how it looks on the day it opens. Finally, think about the books themselves. Libraries are changing, and fewer people borrow printed volumes than before, so your layout should allow shelves to be moved or removed in future without changing the structure.
So we should avoid fixing walls where we might later want an open space. We can use lightweight partitions instead.
Exactly. One last piece of advice. When you build your model, make it at one to fifty rather than one to a hundred, so that the panel can see how people actually move through the entrance.
That makes sense. We'll book the workshop for the model this week.
Please send me the revised drawings by Thursday, and then we can start preparing for the review.

listening.title: Whale migration
listening.titleVi: Tập tính di cư của cá voi
listening.context: A lecturer in marine biology explains why and how large whales migrate, and the threats they now face.

script.say: Part 4. You will hear a lecture on whale migration. First, you have some time to look at questions 31 to 40.

script.t: Good morning, everyone. Today I'd like to talk about one of the most remarkable journeys in the natural world, the annual migration of the great whales. I shall concentrate on humpback whales, because they have been studied the most, but much of what I say applies to other large species as well.

Let's begin with the question that puzzled scientists for a long time. Why would an animal as large as a humpback travel thousands of kilometres every year, when swimming such distances costs an enormous amount of energy? The answer is that the two things a whale needs most are not found in the same place.

In summer, the cold waters near the poles are extremely productive. Long hours of daylight feed tiny plants in the sea, and these in turn feed enormous swarms of krill, which are small shrimp-like animals. A single humpback can swallow tonnes of krill in a day, so for a feeding whale, the polar summer is a banquet.

But that same cold water is a poor place to give birth. A newborn calf has very little blubber, which is the layer of fat that keeps whales warm. So the females travel to warm tropical waters, where the calves can survive until they have built up an insulating layer. The warm water is therefore a nursery, not a restaurant, and that is why the whales must make the journey twice a year.

Now, this creates a problem. While they are in the tropics, the whales find almost nothing to eat. Some individuals live for months on their reserves. By the time an adult returns to the poles, it may have lost as much as twenty-five per cent of its body weight. In other words, the whales are fasting for a large part of the year, which is almost unique among mammals of this size.

Next, how do we know where they go? Until the middle of the last century, the honest answer was that we did not know. Whalers could see where the animals were in summer, but where they spent the winter was a mystery.

Today we have several techniques. The first, and the simplest, is photography. Every humpback has a unique black and white pattern on the underside of its tail, which is known as the fluke, and which works rather like a fingerprint. Researchers photograph each whale when it lifts its tail to dive, and compare the pictures with a catalogue. Over many years, volunteers have collected hundreds of thousands of images.

The second technique is the electronic tag. A small device is fixed to the whale's back with a suction cup or a dart. It records the position of the animal, and each time the whale surfaces, the information is passed on to a satellite, and from there to the laboratory. Some tags have followed a whale for a whole year, and the results have shown that some animals travel more than eight thousand kilometres in one direction.

The third technique is acoustic. Whales are noisy animals, and underwater microphones can pick up their songs from many kilometres away. By placing arrays of microphones along the coast, scientists can count how many whales pass in a season, and even work out which routes they prefer.
The most fascinating question, though, is how they find their way. There is no landmark in the open sea. There are several theories, and I should say at once that none of them has been fully proved.

Some researchers suggested that whales navigate by the sun, but this seems unlikely, because the sun's light is scattered quickly beneath the surface, and whales spend a great deal of time deep in the water. Others think that whales remember the shape of the seabed, a kind of mental map built up over a lifetime. Young animals could learn it by following their mothers.

A third idea is that whales can detect the planet's magnetic pull, rather like a compass. The evidence is indirect. When researchers examined the places where whales had become stranded on beaches, they found that many of these places were where the magnetic field was unusually weak or disturbed. That doesn't prove anything, but it is a suggestive clue, and several laboratories are now testing it.

Whatever the method, one thing is certain. The whales are astonishingly faithful. Calves follow their mothers on the first trip, and then they return to the same feeding area for the rest of their lives, often for fifty years or more. In some places, a feeding area is passed down through families, as if it were an inheritance.

Let me now turn to the threats the whales face today. The first, and perhaps the most obvious, is shipping. Many of the busiest sea lanes cross the whales' routes, and large vessels sometimes strike them. Because the animals spend long periods near the surface when they are resting, a fast container ship may not have time to avoid one. Such encounters often lead to collisions, and the injuries are often fatal.

The second is noise. Engines, drilling and sonar fill the sea with sound, and whales depend on sound for communication, as I said. A male's song can carry for a hundred kilometres in quiet water, but in a noisy harbour it may reach only a tenth of that distance. Mothers and calves, who speak in much softer voices, are especially vulnerable to this.

The third is the changing climate. As the oceans warm, the krill are moving, and they are shifting towards the poles, away from the places where the whales used to find them. Some populations have already responded by changing their schedules. Whales have been seen arriving at feeding grounds weeks earlier, or staying later than they used to, and it is an open question how far such changes can continue.

The picture is not entirely gloomy, however. Several countries have introduced a voluntary speed limit for ships in areas where whales gather, and the number of collisions has fallen where captains actually obey it. Engineers are also developing quieter propellers, and some ports now pay a lower fee to quieter ships.

Meanwhile, after more than half a century of protection from hunting, many populations of humpbacks have recovered. In some regions they are now close to their original numbers, and that is a real success story for conservation. It shows that, given the chance, large whales are able to recover.

To sum up, whale migration is a solution to a problem of geography: food in one place, warmth in another. Studying it has needed patience, new technology and the work of thousands of volunteers, and there is still much to learn about how the animals navigate. In next week's lecture we will look at the smaller whales and dolphins, whose social lives are more complicated than anyone expected.

listening.title: Booking a wedding photographer
listening.titleVi: Đặt thợ chụp ảnh cho đám cưới
listening.context: A man phones a photography studio to book a photographer for his wedding.

script.say: Part 1. You will hear a man phoning a photography studio to book a photographer for his wedding. First, you have some time to look at questions 1 to 6.

script.t: Good afternoon, Fennel Row Photography, Joanne speaking. How can I help?
Hello. My fiancée and I are getting married in the autumn, and we'd like to find out whether you still have a photographer free.
Congratulations! We may well have. I'll open the booking form on my screen and take some details as we go. Could I have your surname, please?
It's Haldane. That's H, A, L, D, A, N, E.
Thank you, Mr Haldane. And which date have you set for the wedding?
The fourteenth of September. We were lucky to get a Saturday.
Lovely. Ah, I'm afraid the fourteenth is already taken. Both of our senior photographers are booked that day.
Oh no. Well, the register office did say they had a space the week after, so we could move everything. Would the twenty-first be possible?
Let me check. Yes, the twenty-first is free, and Ross, our most experienced photographer, is available. Shall I put you down for that?
Please do. I'll tell my fiancée tonight, but I'm sure she'll agree.
Now, where will you be holding the reception? That helps us to plan the lighting, because indoor and outdoor venues are very different.
It's at Heron Barn, just outside the village of Leyton. The ceremony itself is at the register office in town at two o'clock, and then everyone drives out to the barn.
Heron Barn is beautiful, and Ross has worked there before. How many guests are you expecting?
At first we invited a hundred and twenty, but quite a few people have said no, so I think it will be eighty-five. That is the number the caterers are working with, anyway.
Eighty-five. Good. And what sort of photographs do you have in mind? Some couples like formal pictures with everyone lined up, and others prefer something more relaxed.

My parents would love a few formal group photographs, and we'll certainly have those. But personally I dislike stiff poses. I'd much rather have natural pictures of people laughing and chatting, the kind where nobody realises the camera is there.
Candid photography is Ross's speciality, so you're in good hands. I'll make a note that candid shots are the priority, with half an hour set aside for the formal ones.
That sounds perfect.
Finally for this part, a contact number, please.
My mobile is oh double seven double oh, nine one three, four six zero.
Sorry, was that four six zero at the end?
No, I'm sorry, I said it wrongly. It ends four six two.
Four six two. Thank you. I've got everything I need for the form.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 7 to 10.

script.t: Could you tell me about your packages? I saw three on your website, but I'm not sure which would suit us.

Of course. The Bronze package is four hours of coverage, which is really only enough for the ceremony and a few pictures afterwards. Silver gives you six hours, and Gold gives you eight, which means the photographer stays right through the evening party.
I'd love the Gold package, honestly. What does that one cost?
Gold is one thousand three hundred pounds. Silver is nine hundred and fifty.
Hmm. That's quite a difference, and we're already over budget on the catering. If the photographer is there from the ceremony until the speeches, would six hours be enough?
Easily. The speeches are usually over by about eight, and the first dance can be photographed in the same session. Most couples with a reception like yours choose Silver and are very happy with it.
Then I'll go with the Silver package, nine hundred and fifty pounds.
Wonderful. To secure the date we ask for a deposit of two hundred pounds, which comes off the total. The balance is due two weeks before the wedding.
That's fine. Do I pay by card?
Yes, I can take that over the phone once you've agreed the details, or you can do it through our secure payment page.
I'll do it through the website this evening. And how will we receive the photographs afterwards? Do we get prints?

Everything is delivered in a private online gallery, which you and your guests can browse, download and share. It is usually ready about four weeks after the wedding. If you would like the pictures on a memory stick as well, that is an extra forty pounds, but most clients find the gallery is enough.
The gallery will be fine. We can always print our favourites ourselves.
Before the day, Ross likes to meet couples to talk through the schedule. He is usually free on Wednesday evenings, so I'll ask him to call you to arrange a time.
Thank you, Joanne. You've been really helpful.
It's a pleasure. I'll send a confirmation email today. Congratulations again, Mr Haldane, and I hope the weather is kind to you.

listening.title: Home safety and preventing burglary
listening.titleVi: An toàn gia đình và phòng chống trộm
listening.context: A community police officer talks to residents at a neighbourhood meeting about protecting their homes from burglary.

script.say: Part 2. You will hear a community police officer talking to local residents about home safety. First, you have some time to look at questions 11 to 15.

script.t: Good evening, everyone, and thank you for coming out on such a wet night. My name is Dana Whitlock, and I'm the community officer for the Eastfield area. I've been asked to talk to you tonight because burglaries here rose a little over the summer, and I want to explain what you can do to keep your homes safe.

First, a surprise. Most people picture a burglar creeping about in the dark, but in this area the largest number of break-ins happen in the middle of the afternoon, between about one and four, when the houses are empty because everyone is at work or collecting children from school. Night-time burglaries are much rarer, because a burglar does not want to meet anybody.

Second, how do they get in? Many residents imagine smashed windows and broken doors. In fact, the most common way in is simply a door or window that was left unlocked. Over half of the burglaries I dealt with this year involved no force at all. So the first piece of advice is boringly simple: lock up properly every time you leave, even if you are only going next door for ten minutes.

Now, a word about spare keys. Lots of people hide one under a flowerpot or inside a fake rock. Burglars know every one of those hiding places, so please do not use them. Leave a spare key with a neighbour you trust instead. And never leave a key in the lock on the inside of a glass door, because a thief can break the glass and turn it.

Next, the internet. I'm sure many of you enjoy sharing holiday photographs, but if you post pictures while you are still away, you are telling the world that your house is empty. My advice is to wait until you are back, and to check your privacy settings, because even photographs shared with friends can reach people you do not know.

Finally in this section, our neighbourhood watch scheme. At the moment about a third of the households in Eastfield belong to it. It costs nothing to join, and it is not about spying on anybody. Members simply share information by text message, and it works. In the two streets where nearly every house has joined, burglaries have fallen sharply. We would like to reach half of all households by next spring.

script.say: Now look at questions 16 to 20.

script.t: Now I'd like to go round a typical house and talk about each part in turn. Please follow on the leaflet I gave you, which has a drawing of the building.

Let's start at the front door. Most front doors have just one lock, and on many of them the lock is old and easy to force. I recommend fitting a second lock, a good-quality deadlock, about a third of the way up the door. It costs less than most people expect, and it makes a burglar's job far harder. Some people also fit a chain, but a chain only keeps out visitors, not thieves, so please do not rely on it.

Moving to the back of the house, the garden. This is where burglars often work, because they cannot be seen from the road. A light that comes on when it senses movement is cheap to buy and easy to fit, and it is by far the best deterrent. Some residents ask me about tall fences. A high fence can actually help a burglar by hiding him once he is inside, so I would not spend money on that.

Next, the garage. The most valuable items in most garages are bicycles, and those are stolen all the time. Please do not simply stand them against the wall. Fix a ground anchor to the floor, and chain each frame to it with a strong lock. A thief with only a few minutes will usually give up when he sees that.

Then the shed. Garden sheds are usually flimsy, so assume that a determined thief will get in. The sensible response is to make the contents less useful and easier to trace. Mark every power tool and garden tool with your postcode and house number. You can use a special pen that shows up under ultraviolet light, and police officers will recognise those marks straight away. Stolen property that is clearly marked is much harder to sell.

Lastly, the side gate. Many gates are held shut by a simple latch that anyone can lift from the other side. Please fit a padlock and keep it locked, and choose a lock with a hardened shackle that cannot be cut with ordinary tools. I know it is a nuisance to carry a key every time you go to put the bins out, but it makes a real difference.

A few of you asked me before the meeting about two other ideas. Do not trim the hedge down to ground level just to remove hiding places, because a thick hedge at the front also stops people looking into your windows. And I would not bother with fake cameras either. Experienced burglars can tell the difference in seconds, and a genuine camera, even a simple one, is better.

If you remember only one thing tonight, it should be this: burglars are lazy. They look for the easiest house in the street. You do not have to make your home impossible to enter. You only have to make it more trouble than the house next door.

There are tea and biscuits at the back of the hall, and I will stay until nine to answer your questions. Please also take one of the forms for the neighbourhood watch before you leave. Thank you for listening.

listening.title: Planning an essay on the unreliable narrator
listening.titleVi: Lên dàn ý bài luận về người kể chuyện không đáng tin
listening.context: Two literature students discuss an essay plan on an unreliable narrator with their tutor.

script.say: Part 3. You will hear two literature students, Imogen and Kofi, discussing an essay plan with their tutor, Dr Alder. First, you have some time to look at questions 21 to 24.

script.t: Right, let's make a start. Your joint outline on unreliable narrators is on my desk, and I have a few questions. Imogen, why don't you begin by telling me what led you to The Glass Orchard as your main text?

Well, I'd read two other novels by Mairead Tolland, and I liked them, but that wasn't really the reason. What drew me to this book is that the story the narrator tells keeps shifting. Ruth Ames describes the same afternoon three times, and each version is a little different. I wanted to find out why a writer would do that.
That is a good starting point, because it gives you a real question rather than just a topic. Now Kofi, you drafted the title. I have a worry about it.
Is it too long? I did wonder.

Length is not the issue. The title says that you will compare how three novels create unreliable narrators, but you never say what you mean by the word unreliable. Readers use it very loosely. A narrator might lie deliberately, or be confused, or simply see things from a limited viewpoint, and those are quite different things.
So we need a definition at the start?

A working definition, yes, within the first page, so that your argument has something solid to stand on. And with three novels you will only have room for brief summaries, so I would cut it back to two.
I agree with that, actually. I was getting nervous about the word limit.
Which second novel would you keep? Choose one whose narrator contrasts with Ruth, so that the comparison is sharp and gives you plenty to say.
Probably the book by Idris Vane, where the narrator is a young detective who is convinced she is always right.

That would work well. Her confidence is a kind of unreliability too, since she ignores any evidence that does not suit her theory, and readers trust her at first precisely because she sounds so sure of herself.
I hadn't thought of certainty as a warning sign. That's a fascinating point, and it gives us a real contrast to build the whole argument on.
Tell me what you think is going on with Ruth. Is she deceiving the reader?
I think she is. She hides things on purpose, because she is ashamed of what she did in the house.

I'm not so sure. To me it seems more likely that her memory is failing. She is eighty years old when she tells the story, and she even says that she cannot trust her own recollections. Surely that makes her honest rather than deceitful.
That disagreement could be the heart of your essay, so don't hide it. Argue it out openly, with evidence from the text for each view.
We did find an article by a critic called Hal Norwood that supports my reading. He says the author intends us to distrust Ruth from the first page.

I know the article. I would be careful with it. He writes with great confidence, but when you look closely he is mostly guessing what Tolland meant, and he offers very little proof from the novel itself. I would use it as an opinion to discuss, not as authority.

script.say: Now look at questions 25 and 26.

script.t: We've also been trying to list the ways the novel makes readers doubt Ruth. At first we thought the dates in her account did not match.
I checked that, and the chronology is perfectly consistent, so you can drop it. The author does use two other devices, though, and they are worth explaining carefully.
One is that other characters give a different version of events. The gardener, for instance, says he was never in the house that afternoon.
Exactly. And the second?
The letters. Ruth quotes from letters she says she received, but when the letters appear in full a few chapters later, they say something rather different.

Yes, that is the most striking example. Some critics also point to the shifts of tense, but I think that is a distraction. Do not make too much of it. There are no editor's notes in this edition, so you cannot use those either.

script.say: Before you hear the rest of the conversation, you have some time to look at questions 27 to 30.

script.t: Let's go through the plan section by section. Your introduction first. It runs to nearly four hundred words, and most of that is the plot of the book.
I thought the examiners would need to know the story.
They already know it. Give them two sentences of context and spend the rest of the space on your argument. At the moment it reads like a book report.
OK. The next section is on the narrative voice, where we look at how Ruth talks to the reader.
That section is the strongest part. You have chosen quotations that really show her habit of speaking directly to the reader and then taking things back. Keep it just as it is.
Thank you. The third section is about the ending, where she finally admits that the first version was false.

There you make a big claim, that the ending proves she was lying from the start. But you give one example only, and it is a short quotation. One more passage from the final chapter would make the case much stronger.
I can add the scene with the broken clock. That works.

Good. And your conclusion simply repeats what you have already said. What you need there is a clear answer to the question you asked at the beginning, which is why a writer would choose such a narrator in the first place.
So we say what the effect on the reader is, not just what the author does.
Precisely. Make the reader's experience your last point.
How many sources do you expect us to use?
Five or six reliable ones is plenty. Quality matters more than quantity. And please check every page reference at the end, because that is where students lose marks for no good reason.
Should we send the plan by email, or bring a printed copy?
Email is fine, and please put your names and the module code at the top of the document, because I mark a great many of these.
We will send you the revised plan on Thursday.
Good. Then we can fix the deadline for the first draft when we meet next week.

options: She had enjoyed other books by the same author.

items.explain: Imogen đã đọc 2 cuốn khác của tác giả nhưng nói đó không phải lý do thật; điều cuốn hút cô là lời kể của Ruth liên tục thay đổi. Câu nghe được: “the story the narrator tells keeps shifting”. → B

options: It is longer than it should be.

items.explain: Tiêu đề không giải thích “unreliable” nghĩa là gì; độ dài không phải vấn đề. Câu nghe được: “you never say what you mean by the word unreliable”. → A

items.q: What is Kofi’s opinion of Ruth?
options: She may simply be forgetting things.
She is deliberately hiding the truth.
The reader should not judge her.
items.cue: it seems more likely that her memory is failing
items.explain: Imogen nghĩ Ruth cố tình che giấu; Kofi lại cho rằng trí nhớ của bà đang suy giảm nên bà thành thật chứ không lừa dối. Câu nghe được: “it seems more likely that her memory is failing”. → C

items.q: What does Dr Alder think of the article by Hal Norwood?
options: It rests mainly on guesses about the author’s intention.
It gives the most reliable evidence available.
